signals.title: Brazil's New National Migration, Refuge and Statelessness Policy Mandates Basic-Education and Childcare Access for Migrant and Refugee Children
signals.summary: Brazil promulgated Decree No. 12.657 on 7 October 2025 (published 8 October 2025), instituting the National Policy on Migration, Refuge and Statelessness that regulates Article 120 of the 2017 Migration Law (Lei 13.445/2017). Its education provisions (Art. 12) task the Ministry of Education, within the policy, with monitoring access to compulsory basic education — including adult/youth education tracks and creches (nurseries) subject to available places — for migrant, refugee and stateless students; supporting intercultural and bilingual/multilingual schooling in border regions and areas with high concentrations of such students (including Indigenous migrant, refugee and stateless children); expanding entry, retention and completion across basic, technical and higher education; and standardising simplified enrolment, study-equivalence and credential-recognition procedures. The decree also amends Decree 9.199/2017, the regulation of the Migration Law.

signals.title: US states advance 2026 wave of juvenile solitary-confinement limits as Maryland House passes restrictive-housing curbs 104-31
signals.summary: In the 2026 legislative sessions, several US states moved to ban or sharply restrict solitary confinement of children in juvenile facilities. Maryland's House Bill 921 (Juvenile Law - Confinement and Restrictive Housing - Limitations) passed the House of Delegates 104-31 on 10 March 2026 and advanced to the Senate; it bars placing a minor in restrictive housing solely for discipline, punishment, administrative convenience, retaliation or staffing shortages, permits locked-door seclusion only as a temporary measure on clear-and-convincing evidence of immediate risk, and carries a 1 October 2026 proposed effective date. New York's 'Keep Kids Out of Solitary Confinement Act' (A07414/S03885) would codify a statutory ban on segregated confinement - defined as cell confinement exceeding 17 hours a day - for children in detention facilities, and South Dakota's HB1276 sought to limit juvenile isolation to immediate-danger situations before being deferred in committee in February 2026.
signals.why_it_matters: This is a concrete child-vs-justice-system governance fight over one of the most damaging practices minors face in custody: prolonged isolation, which the UN Special Rapporteur on Torture treats as torture and which is especially harmful to the developing adolescent brain. Moving solitary from a discretionary disciplinary tool to a tightly limited last resort operationalises the principle that detained children remain children owed developmental protection, not punitive adults. For intergenerational equity and foresight, the clustered 2026 state activity - one chamber-passed bill, one codification effort, one failed bill - maps the uneven, sub-national pace at which the anti-solitary norm is hardening into enforceable law, and pairs with MACR raises and diversion reforms as part of a broader push to make child custody less harmful.

signals.title: Maryland enacts SB162, extending sentence-review rights to all children after abolishing juvenile life without parole
signals.summary: On 12 May 2026 Maryland Governor Wes Moore signed Senate Bill 162, a bipartisan measure confirming that the sentence-review provisions of the 2021 Juvenile Restoration Act (JRA) apply to children sentenced after 1 October 2021, not only those sentenced before. The JRA had abolished life without parole for children and let judges review sentences of people who committed offences under age 18; SB162 closes a gap so that every person imprisoned in Maryland for a childhood offence can seek sentencing review after serving 20 years. The change lands as national advocates mark a decade since Montgomery v. Louisiana, with 28 states and the District of Columbia now banning juvenile life without parole and roughly 1,300 people sentenced to JLWOP as children released nationwide.
signals.why_it_matters: This is a clean child-vs-justice signal: it treats even children who committed the most serious offences as capable of change and entitled to a meaningful second look, rather than permanent condemnation - the core of the US Supreme Court's Miller/Montgomery line. For intergenerational equity, guaranteed review after 20 years converts 'no child is irredeemable' from rhetoric into an enforceable procedural right, giving incarcerated young people hope and a pathway home while a Montclair State study of released JLWOP cohorts found a 1.14% recidivism rate. Tracked with the ACT/Victoria MACR raises, Maryland's own 2026 raise-the-age charging reform, and Scotland's ending of child imprisonment, it evidences a sustained 2025-2026 move to dismantle the harshest punishments imposed on children.

signals.title: US states embed restorative-justice diversion for youth as Vermont funds statewide pre-charge programme for the first time in 2026
signals.summary: A 2026 review by The Sentencing Project documents a wave of US states moving restorative-justice (RJ) diversion for children from an optional, aspirational practice toward a funded, standardised element of the youth justice system. Vermont will for the first time in 2026 provide dedicated funds for pre-charge restorative-justice diversion, allocating $1.2 million in year one to support youth (and adult) diversion programmes across 14 of the state's 16 counties, while Connecticut issued new protocols in 2025 making restorative justice a core element of diversion programmes statewide after training more than 2,000 staff and volunteers. The report also highlights a 2026 University of Minnesota evaluation of Ramsey County (St. Paul), where youth diverted into restorative justice for first-time assault charges were two-thirds less likely to reoffend than those processed in juvenile court.

It complements diversion-over-detention reforms in England and Wales and the UN Committee's diversion guidance, showing the child-justice frontier moving beyond raising the age toward what replaces prosecution.

signals.title: UK evaluation finds Cyber Choices diversion roughly halves online reoffending as programme scales child-focused prevention in 2026
signals.summary: The UK's Cyber Choices programme - a National Crime Agency and police-led early-intervention scheme that diverts children and young people away from cyber-dependent crime under the Computer Misuse Act 1990 - gained fresh evidence and reach in 2026. signals.title: Scotland ends imprisonment of under-18s under Children (Care and Justice) Act as first annual review tracks shift to secure care
signals.summary: Scotland's Children (Care and Justice) (Scotland) Act 2024 has ended the detention of under-18s in Young Offenders' Institutions and prisons, effectively capping child deprivation of liberty to secure-care settings. Commencement regulations that took effect on 28 August 2024 stopped new admissions of children under 18 to YOIs and required all remaining under-18s at YOI Polmont to be moved to secure care, with the Scottish Government funding remand placements during transition; further provisions - including a fuller definition of 'child' for court-ordered detention - commenced on 5 May 2025. The Scottish Government has published a first annual report reviewing the Act's operation over 2024-2025, and additional provisions on the Children's Hearings System, children in police custody and secure transport are anticipated to commence from early 2026.

Prompted by deaths of young people in custody and framed around the UNCRC and Scotland's 'Keep the Promise' commitment, it operationalises detention as a genuine last resort in a child-appropriate setting, a direct intergenerational-equity intervention given how strongly childhood imprisonment predicts lifelong harm. Tracked alongside the England and Wales youth justice White Paper, Australian MACR raises and the UN Committee's last-resort-detention findings, Scotland provides a live natural experiment in abolishing child imprisonment nationwide and shifting spend toward secure, rehabilitative care.

signals.title: Iran Re-enters UN Child-Rights Review Cycle as OHCHR Publishes Its Fifth–Sixth Periodic Report With Sharia Reservation Intact
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: The UN Committee on the Rights of the Child officially published Iran's combined fifth and sixth periodic reports (CRC/C/IRN/5-6) on 18 November 2025, formally reopening Iran's treaty-body examination for the first time since its last review concluded in 2016. The report reiterates in its introduction that the Convention's provisions bind Iran only insofar as they conform to Sharia criteria and domestic legislation, preserving Iran's sweeping general reservation. signals.title: Hungary Writes Child Protection Into Its Constitution as a Right Overriding All Others Except the Right to Life
signals.summary: On 14 April 2025 the Hungarian Parliament passed, and President Sulyok signed, the 15th Amendment to the Fundamental Law (Hungary's constitution), which enshrines a child's right to the protection and care necessary for physical, mental and moral development and declares that this right takes precedence over all other fundamental rights except the right to life. The same amendment package also constitutionalised other measures (the right to pay with cash and provisions on suspending citizenship). Legal analysts note the child-rights clause, while framed in the language of the best interests of the child, is coupled with the existing constitutional obligation to secure children an upbringing 'in accordance with the constitutional identity and Christian culture' of Hungary and to protect a self-identity 'corresponding to their sex at birth'.

But it is also a cautionary signal for the child-rights field – the same clause is being used to justify restricting children's access to information on gender and same-sex relationships, running counter to ECtHR case law (Macáté v Lithuania). It shows how the 'best interests of the child' frame can be constitutionalised to advance illiberal aims, a tension foresight analysts must track as more states consider embedding children's rights in basic law.

signals.title: European Court of Human Rights: Courts Must Consider Hearing the Child Before Ordering an Abduction Return
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: In a Chamber judgment notified in September 2025 (M.P. and Others v. Greece, application no. 2068/24), the European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights where Greek courts ordered two children returned to the United States under the 1980 Hague Child Abduction Convention without considering, of their own motion, whether to ascertain the children's views. The Court held that domestic courts are under a procedural duty, inherent in Article 8 and in their obligation to act in the children's best interests, to examine whether it is appropriate to hear the child before ruling on return – even absent an express request – in order to rule out any 'grave risk' under Article 13(1)(b). The forcible return was therefore not 'necessary in a democratic society'.

signals.title: Brazil's Supreme Court Reads the Hague Abduction Convention Through the Constitution's Best-Interests Principle

signals.title: Colombia's Constitutional Court Rules the Child's Best Interests Override Parents' Refusal to Vaccinate

signals.title: India's Supreme Court Frames Child-Centric Limits on Psychological Testing of Children in Custody Disputes
signals.summary: On 11 June 2026 the Supreme Court of India, in Sheetal Vasant Thakur v. Chirag Arora (2026 INSC 638; Justices Sanjay Karol and N. signals.title: Germany Approves 34-Measure Economic Package with Pension Reform, Tax Relief, and Intergenerational Fairness Framing
signals.summary: On 2 July 2026, Chancellor Friedrich Merz's CDU/CSU–SPD coalition agreed a 34-measure reform package covering pensions, tax, labour and bureaucracy. Tax: about €10bn annual relief for lower/middle incomes partly funded by raising the top rate. In his 9 July Bundestag policy statement, Merz said the aim is to 'restore a fair balance between the generations' and use capital-market opportunities so contribution rates fall and provision standards rise over time. Legislation is still pending; public support for intergenerational-fairness claims is weak in early July polling.

signals.title: Harsant PhD Synthesis Finds Local Government Youth Impact Depends on Decision-Maker Buy-In and Feedback Loops, Not Council Structure Alone

Its finding that impact is relational and contingent on adult responsiveness and institutional feedback loops directly challenges the assumption that creating youth councils satisfies intergenerational equity obligations. For foresight, it offers an evaluative checklist: track buy-in, agenda-setting power, and feedback mechanisms, not just council existence.

signals.title: Global Youth Participation Index 2025: Socio-Economic Barriers Score Highest but Strong Economy Does Not Guarantee Civic or Political Inclusion
signals.summary: The Global Youth Participation Index (GYPI) 2025, launched mid-June 2025 by the European Partnership for Democracy under the EU WYDE Civic Engagement programme with University of Birmingham-linked researchers and a nine-member Youth Panel, is the first systematic global index scoring 141 countries (85%+ data coverage of 41 variables) on youth participation. Four unweighted dimensions average to an overall 0–100 score: Socio-Economic (6 vars, global avg ~77), Civic Space (11, avg 62), Elections (13, avg 54) and Political Affairs (11, avg 51—the weakest). Global overall average is 61; Norway and New Zealand lead at 84; Afghanistan is last at 14. The index draws multi-source data (including the Youth Progress Index) plus 66 country consultants. Core claim: low scores measure structural barriers and closed opportunity structures, not youth apathy—youth legislative representation averages only about 12/100 and 28 countries have zero youth MPs. High socio-economic scores do not guarantee high overall GYPI (e.g. Czechia, Singapore). Nuance: GYPI measures enabling structures more than absolute activism levels; social-movement and online-debate volume remain gaps; influence of participation on policy is not scored.

signals.title: Bank of Korea Finds Youth Job-Search Delays and Housing Costs Permanently Scar Lifetime Earnings

signals.summary: Bank of Korea Issue Note 2026-2, published 12 February 2026, quantifies how delayed labour-market entry and housing-cost burdens compound across young Koreans' lifetimes. signals.title: Nigerian Senate Passes Constitutional State Police Bill With Safeguards Against Political Weaponisation
signals.summary: On 24 June 2026, the Nigerian Senate passed the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria (Alteration) (State Police) Bill, 2026 (SB. 1055), establishing a dual Federal Police Service and State Police Services framework. More than two-thirds of senators voted in favour after clause-by-clause consideration. The bill empowers governors to appoint state commissioners subject to state assembly confirmation, prohibits using state police against government critics, requires stated cause and two-thirds assembly approval to remove commissioners, and mandates State Police Service Commissions for recruitment, discipline and complaints oversight. Existing regional outfits such as Amotekun and Hisbah cannot automatically become state police or bear firearms. The amendment still requires concurrence and ratification by at least 24 of 36 state assemblies.

signals.title: Portugal Publishes Updated Intergenerational Justice Index Across Six Policy Dimensions
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: In November 2025 the Institute of Public Policy (IPP–Lisbon), with Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation support, published the updated Intergenerational Justice Index (IJI) for Portugal (presented 4 December 2025 at the Gulbenkian Foundation). The annual composite tracks six equal-weight dimensions—environment and natural resources, health, labour market, housing, poverty and living conditions, and public finances—normalised to (0,1], with movement toward 1 meaning relative improvement for younger and future cohorts. After mild aggregate improvement through about 2020, the 2016–2023 update shows a reversal in 2022–23 driven mainly by housing (price-to-income accessibility and share of 25–34-year-olds living with parents; housing sub-index reported falling from roughly 0.46 in 2019 to 0.23 in 2023) and health (unmet needs, household out-of-pocket spending, anxiolytic/antidepressant use), with a milder public-finance drag. Labour market and poverty dimensions improve modestly; environment shows slight net gain. Nuance: the index is diachronic for Portugal only, not a cross-country ranking; absolute levels matter less than annual change; public-finance methodology was redesigned in 2025 (from generational accounts toward explicit debt plus implicit pension liabilities and capital stock) and back-applied for series consistency; many indicators are youth-age or trend proxies rather than full-life cohort microdata.
signals.why_it_matters: Portugal offers a national multi-domain measurement model for intergenerational equity without a future-generations commissioner: a public dashboard that makes housing, fiscal liabilities, environment, health, labour and poverty jointly visible. The 2025 reversal—especially the housing collapse—shows IE can deteriorate even when some social indicators improve, reinforcing the platform rule that aggregates must be read component-wise. For GYC framework design, the IJI supplies equal-weight geometric aggregation practice, the sustainability-vs-justice distinction, and Layer C–D indicators (housing autonomy, implicit pension liabilities) that complement the Youth Progress Index (global youth rights) and JRC same-age cohort income/housing method. It was cited as a replicable member-state tool around the Group of Friends of Future Generations and parallels the EU Intergenerational Fairness Index under construction.

signals.title: Montana Youth Civic Organizations Sue State Over SB 490 and SB 276, Alleging Unconstitutional Burdens on Young Voters

signals.title: Montana Supreme Court Advances Direct Democracy Protection Ballot Measure After Attorney General Block
signals.summary: On 27 February 2026, the Montana Supreme Court reversed Attorney General Austin Knudsen's determination in Kendrick v. The measure would create express constitutional protections for the right of initiative and referendum, limit legislative ability to burden that right, prevent government officials from showing partiality for or against ballot measures, and ensure adequate time for signature gathering. The ruling followed legislative efforts to make it harder for citizens to amend the constitution, including the nation's highest initiative filing fee ($3,700), expanded attorney general review powers, and a requirement that the AG assess whether proposals would cause 'significant material harm' to business interests. The Kendrick ruling preserves the 2026 ballot pathway for constitutional protection of direct democracy at a moment when Montana's legislature has simultaneously restricted youth voting access (SB 490/SB 276) and attempted to limit climate litigation venue (SB 97). The measure, if passed, would constitutionally insulate the initiative process from future legislative burdening — an institutional safeguard for intergenerational voice that does not depend on which party controls the legislature. policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: A CNBC analysis published on 24 June 2026, drawing on UBS data, reports that an estimated $83.5 trillion will pass from baby boomers and older entrepreneurs to their children and grandchildren over the next two decades, the largest wealth transfer in modern history. Billionaire families alone are expected to transfer $6.9 trillion by 2040. Younger heirs are more internationally educated, more mobile, and more open to diversified investments across asset classes and markets than the builder generation. Natixis surveys show 78% of millennial investors in Asia-Pacific want market-beating opportunities (versus 38% of baby boomers), 53% seek private assets, and 62% discuss cryptocurrency with advisers. signals.title: US Senator Murphy Introduces Living Wage For All Act to Raise Federal Minimum Wage to $25
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: On 25 June 2026, US Senator Chris Murphy (D-CT) introduced the Living Wage For All Act, bicameral legislation to raise the federal minimum wage to $25 per hour. Under a two-track phase-in, large corporate employers would be required to implement a $25 wage floor by 2032, while other businesses would have until 2039. The bill also mandates automatic continued increases pegged to two-thirds of the national median wage, and phases out subminimum wages for tipped workers, workers with disabilities, and youth workers. Co-sponsors include Senators Blumenthal, Kim, and Wyden, with companion House legislation from Representatives Ramirez, Mejia, Garcia, and Simon. The federal minimum wage has not been raised since 2009.
signals.why_it_matters: This is a structurally intergenerational bill even though it is not framed primarily in those terms. Young and entry-level workers are disproportionately concentrated in minimum-wage and subminimum-wage employment, and a $25 floor with automatic indexation changes the lifetime earnings trajectory for cohorts entering the workforce now. The phase-out of youth subminimum wages is a direct intergenerational fairness intervention, removing a legal structure that explicitly permitted younger workers to be paid less for the same work. The bill also represents a shift from episodic congressional wage-setting to automatic indexation, which reduces the political risk that future generations will inherit a stagnant wage floor.

signals.title: Hawaii Joins U.S. Climate Alliance Affordable Clean Cars Coalition, Deepening Subnational Clean Transportation Diplomacy
signals.summary: On 4 September 2025, Hawaii Governor Josh Green joined the U.S. Climate Alliance's Affordable Clean Cars Coalition, a 13-governor partnership launched to sustain America's transition to cleaner and more affordable vehicles and safeguard states' clean air authority following Congress's revocation of California's vehicle emission rules. Hawaii has been an original member of the U.S. Climate Alliance since its founding on 1 June 2017 alongside California, New York, and Washington — formed in direct response to the first U.S. withdrawal from the Paris Agreement. The Alliance now represents 24 governors covering approximately 60% of the U.S. population and economy. The Affordable Clean Cars Coalition focuses on reducing cost barriers to EVs, expanding charging infrastructure, exploring next-generation low-carbon fuel policies, and defending states' Clean Air Act authority to adopt transportation solutions independently of federal policy.
signals.why_it_matters: Hawaii's U.S. Climate Alliance membership and participation in the Affordable Clean Cars Coalition directly fills the international commitments gap for Hawaii: as a non-sovereign subnational jurisdiction, Hawaii's primary international climate commitment mechanism is through multi-state coalitions acting as de facto climate diplomacy when the federal government has withdrawn from the Paris Agreement and the UNFCCC. The intergenerational mechanism is structural: Alliance states represent 60% of the U.S. economy and their coordinated clean transportation policies lock in emissions reduction trajectories that protect future generations irrespective of federal policy volatility. The Affordable Clean Cars Coalition is particularly significant for Hawaii given the state's extreme dependence on imported petroleum for transportation and its Navahine settlement-mandated zero-emission ground transportation by 2045. The coalition's defense of state clean air authority also protects the regulatory architecture enabling Hawaii's clean fuel standard and transportation decarbonization targets. signals.title: UHERO Report Analyzes Costs of Hawaiian Electric's Full Clean Energy Transition Under 'Hawaii Powered' Initiative
signals.summary: In late June 2026, the University of Hawaii Economic Research Organization (UHERO) released a report analyzing the costs and implementation steps required for Hawaiian Electric's full transition to 100% clean energy under the utility's 'Hawaii Powered' initiative. The report examines projected rate impacts, infrastructure investments, and timeline feasibility of achieving the state's 2045 renewable energy mandate, including costs of grid modernization, energy storage deployment, and the phaseout of fossil-fuel generation across Oahu, Maui, and Hawaii Island. The utility simultaneously unveiled its Hawaii Powered vision, encouraging public input on the 100% local clean energy plan. The analysis arrives amid ongoing debate over Act 24's cap on solar tax credits, warnings from advocates that the cap will stall clean energy momentum, and Governor Green's Executive Order 26-02 temporarily preserving 2026 tax credits.
signals.why_it_matters: The UHERO report operationalizes the intergenerational cost distribution question at the heart of Hawaii's energy transition: who pays for the clean energy infrastructure that future generations will depend on? The mechanism — an independent economic analysis of ratepayer impacts over the transition timeline — informs whether Hawaii's renewable energy mandate will produce affordable electricity for younger households or impose disproportionate rate burdens on them to fund infrastructure from which current homeowners (via rooftop solar) already benefit. The report arrives at a critical juncture: Act 24's solar tax credit phaseout threatens to slow the rooftop solar adoption that has historically reduced grid costs for all ratepayers including renters, while Hawaii ranks first nationally in per capita rooftop solar with nearly half of households having systems. The 'Hawaii Powered' planning process, combined with UHERO's cost analysis, creates an evidence base for intergenerational rate design. It warns that compliance-heavy governance looks backward while strategy needs to look forward, and that whatever forward-looking work happens gets quietly delegated to risk committees, which by definition focus on what could go wrong rather than what a company might want to become. signals.title: US Student Debt Repayment System Overhauled as Save Plan Dismantled, Affecting 7 Million Borrowers
signals.summary: The Reimagining and Improving Student Education (RISE) final regulations, published 1 May 2026 (Federal Register 2026-08556) and posted to FSA Partners on 4 May, implement Public Law 119-21 for Title IV loans. From 1 July 2026 new Direct Loan borrowers may use only the Repayment Assistance Plan (RAP) or a new Tiered Standard plan (10-25 years by balance). RAP sets payments at 1-10% of income minus $50 per dependent, with a $10 minimum, an on-time unpaid-interest waiver, a matching principal payment of up to $50, and remaining-balance discharge after 360 on-time payments (30 years). Existing ICR/PAYE/SAVE plans sunset by 1 July 2028. The same package phases out Grad PLUS and imposes new graduate, professional and Parent PLUS limits. An ED fact sheet dated 9 June 2026 confirms RAP and Tiered Standard opened 1 July 2026. A 24 June 2026 D.D.C. preliminary stay temporarily altered the professional-degree list used for those loan caps; FSA said on 10 July that Grad PLUS elimination, the new limits and the two repayment plans still took effect 1 July.

signals.summary: The Crow Revenue Act (H.R. 725), introduced by Rep. Troy Downing (MT-02) and Sen. Steve Daines (R-MT), was reported favorably out of the House Natural Resources Committee with bipartisan support in January 2026. The bill would transfer approximately 4,660 acres of private subsurface interests on the Crow Reservation to the Crow Tribe, while the Hope Family Trust would receive about 4,530 acres of federal subsurface interests and 940 acres of federal surface interests in the Bull Mountains. The land exchange is designed to consolidate tribal mineral interests and ensure the long-term viability of Signal Peak Energy's Bull Mountains coal mine. Musselshell County Commissioner Robert Pancratz calculated the county could lose up to $11.6 million in tax revenue under the bill as written. Pancratz was defeated in the June 2026 Republican primary after advocating for diversification planning, with the Crow Revenue Act as the central issue. The Trump administration approved the mining plan modification for the Bull Mountains mine on June 6, 2026, as a short-term measure while the legislation advances.
signals.why_it_matters: The Crow Revenue Act is a concentrated intergenerational equity conflict at the intersection of tribal sovereignty, fossil fuel extraction, and local fiscal sustainability. The mechanism — a federal land exchange that transfers coal-bearing subsurface rights — determines who captures the remaining value of a non-renewable resource and who bears the transition costs when the resource is depleted. For the Crow Tribe, the bill offers revenue generation and tribal self-determination. For Musselshell County, it threatens the loss of federal mineral revenue that funds local services for current and future residents. The electoral defeat of Commissioner Pancratz, who raised the long-term planning question, demonstrates the political economy of intergenerational governance: the costs of planning for a post-coal future are borne immediately by elected officials, while the benefits accrue to younger and future generations. Relationship memory: connects to the Montana coal deregulation package signal (severance tax cuts), the Coal Tax Trust Fund cap debate, the Musselshell County commissioner defeat signal, and the broader pattern of fossil fuel-dependent jurisdictions managing just transition governance.

signals.title: UK Treasury Committee Finds Government Mis-Sold Student Loans to a Generation, Calls Interest Rate System 'Broken and Unfair'
signals.summary: The UK House of Commons Treasury Committee published a report on 6 July 2026 finding that the government mis-sold student loans to a generation by using a 'statistically flawed' RPI measure of inflation to set interest rates, causing graduate debts to grow faster than necessary. The report concludes the income-contingent interest rate system is 'broken and unfair,' noting that from 2030 RPI will be merged with CPIH but this will be 'little consolation to students who have had their loans inflated by a flawed measure for in some cases almost two decades.' The Committee argued the government has a 'moral duty' to reverse the April 2027 Plan 2 repayment threshold freeze and called the continued use of RPI 'regrettable,' having first recommended switching to CPI in 2018. Average debt among borrowers who finished their course in 2023 was £47,900 when they first became liable to repay in April 2026.
signals.why_it_matters: This is a rare instance of a parliamentary committee explicitly using 'mis-sold' language about a government programme that directly shapes the lifetime wealth trajectory of an entire generation. The student loan system is a structural intergenerational wealth transfer mechanism: graduates (disproportionately younger cohorts) carry debt inflated by a flawed index while older generations benefited from free or heavily subsidised higher education. The report's finding that the government has a 'moral duty' to act, even if not legally liable, frames intergenerational fairness as a binding political obligation rather than a discretionary policy choice. The £47,900 average debt figure quantifies the scale of the burden being placed on young people entering the workforce. Relationship memory: connects to the broader intergenerational-fiscal-policy trend (Australia tax reform, Germany pension reform, UK social care funding) and to the growing evidence base on how higher education finance systems distribute lifetime costs and benefits across generations.

signals.title: Hawaii SB3000 Fossil Fuel Accountability Bill Dies in Senate Ways and Means Committee, Shifting Climate Cost Recovery to Courts
signals.summary: Hawaii Senate Bill 3000, which would have authorized the state and insurance providers to sue fossil fuel companies for climate-driven disaster costs and insurance premium increases, died on 4 March 2026 when the Senate Ways and Means Committee voted it down. The bill had passed the Senate Commerce and Consumer Protection Committee in February 2026 with strong community testimony from 82 individuals and organizations. The measure was part of a coordinated legislative push across California, Hawaii, and New York to make fossil fuel companies pay for climate-driven insurance rate hikes. Its failure leaves Hawaii's climate cost recovery efforts to the existing state tort lawsuit against oil and gas companies, which survived a federal preemption challenge in April 2026 when the U.S. District Court dismissed with prejudice the DOJ's attempt to block the state's climate deception claims.
signals.why_it_matters: SB3000's failure represents a significant legislative gap in Hawaii's climate accountability architecture: the state has a dedicated climate resilience funding mechanism (the Green Fee taxing tourists) and a surviving tort lawsuit against fossil fuel companies, but lacks a statutory framework to systematically recover climate-driven insurance costs from the fossil fuel industry. The intergenerational equity mechanism the bill would have created is direct: it would have shifted the rising cost of climate-driven insurance premiums - which disproportionately burden younger homeowners and renters - from policyholders back to the fossil fuel companies whose products caused the damage. The bill's defeat in committee, despite broad public support, illustrates the political difficulty of legislating fossil fuel accountability even in a state with strong climate governance institutions. The surviving tort route through state courts is slower, case-by-case, and faces ongoing federal preemption challenges, meaning the intergenerational cost shift the bill aimed to achieve remains incomplete. Relationship memory: connects to Hawaii's climate deception lawsuit against oil companies (which survived DOJ preemption challenge), the Green Fee's tourism-tax resilience funding, and the parallel legislative efforts in California and New York.

scores.rationale: A useful counter-signal showing the political limits of fossil-fuel cost-recovery legislation despite broad testimony support — the failure is instructive, but the underlying tort route continues via courts.

signals.title: Hawaii Climate Commission Finalizes Climate Action Pathways, Operationalizing 2045 Net-Zero Commitment Through Community-Driven Sector Plans

The plan was developed through a multi-year participatory process rooted in the principle of malama aina - caring for land and ecosystems to ensure a thriving future. CCMAC, established by Act 32 in 2017, serves as the primary coordinating body for climate action across 20 departments, committees, and counties, co-chaired by DLNR and the Office of Planning and Sustainable Development.

The mechanism - a multi-stakeholder commission with statutory authority producing sector-specific action pathways - creates institutional durability that outlasts electoral cycles, making it harder for future policymakers to back away from 2045 commitments. signals.title: Hawaii House Committee Advances LNG Guardrails Bill, Rejecting Full Ban in Favor of Environmental Safeguards for Future Energy Decisions

signals.title: Allies of Incoming UK PM Burnham Examine Scrapping CGT Uplift on Death, Framed as Intergenerational Fairness Reform
signals.summary: In late June and early July 2026, reports emerged that figures close to incoming UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, including Cabinet ally Louise Haigh, have been examining a review of the Capital Gains Tax (CGT) uplift that currently applies when someone inherits an asset. Under current rules, inherited assets receive a 'base cost' uplift to their market value at the date of death, meaning capital gains accrued during the deceased's lifetime escape CGT entirely. Haigh has argued that any wider review of the tax system should at minimum look at reforming this uplift, and has separately described the present Inheritance Tax system as raising 'fair questions about intergenerational fairness.' The reform consideration comes as Burnham prepares to take office with an explicit intergenerational fairness agenda, including proposed income tax breaks for young homebuyers and Land Value Tax exploration.
signals.why_it_matters: The CGT uplift on death is one of the most consequential and least-discussed intergenerational wealth transfer mechanisms in the UK tax system. It allows billions in capital gains accrued during a lifetime to pass tax-free to heirs, disproportionately benefiting wealthier families who hold appreciating assets (property, shares) across generations. Scrapping the uplift would represent a structural reform to how intergenerational wealth transfers are taxed — closing a loophole that effectively privileges inherited wealth over earned income. The fact that this is being considered by the incoming Burnham government, which has explicitly adopted intergenerational fairness as a governing framework, signals that wealth transfer taxation may become a live policy front in the UK. The reform would align the UK more closely with other OECD countries that tax capital gains at death. Relationship memory: connects to the existing UK intergenerational fiscal reform cluster (IFS inheritance tax analysis, Intergenerational Foundation Burnham fiscal inheritance report, Burnham Gen Z tax relief proposal) and the broader global trend toward wealth transfer taxation as an intergenerational equity tool.

signals.title: Article 109 Charter Review Momentum Builds: Romania, Kyrgyzstan, India, Kazakhstan Signal Support for UN Charter Review Conference
signals.summary: Article 109 of the UN Charter — which allows a general review conference to be convened by a two-thirds vote of the General Assembly and any nine Security Council members, with no P5 veto — is gaining unprecedented momentum in 2026. In the last six weeks, Romania called for invoking Article 109 at the General Assembly, India discussed the mandate for Charter review at the Security Council, and Andorra asked Security Council candidates whether it was time to revise the Charter. Germany remarked that the Article 109 initiative is 'interesting' and worth considering. Kyrgyzstan's President Zhaparov instructed diplomats to begin considering possible amendments and table them in September 2026. Kazakhstan and The Gambia have officially endorsed Article 109. Brazil, India, and South Africa (IBSA) jointly urged convening a review conference under Article 109. At the 2025 UNGA, 148 countries representing 78% of UN membership called for UN reform. The Article 109 Coalition (article109.org) is coordinating civil society advocacy around the pathway, which was written into the Charter in 1945 as a compromise to smaller powers who accepted the P5 veto only temporarily.
signals.why_it_matters: Article 109 is the only Charter amendment pathway that cannot be vetoed by the P5 at the convening stage — a review conference can be triggered by a two-thirds GA vote plus any nine Security Council members. After 81 years without a review conference, the 2026 surge in state endorsements (Romania, Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan, Gambia, IBSA) signals that the 'San Francisco promise' may finally be fulfilled. For intergenerational equity advocates, a Charter review conference would be the most consequential governance reform opportunity in decades — potentially reshaping Security Council composition, veto powers, and the legal framework for future generations. The C4UNWN GFF Futures Lab workshop on July 11 is directly connected to this momentum, using Article 109 as one of the key reform tracks in its present-forward methodology.

signals.title: UN80 Workstream II Mandate Review Advances: Ad-Hoc Working Group Developing Tools to Assess and Retire GA Mandates
signals.summary: The UN80 Initiative's Workstream II (Mandates) is making progress through the Ad-Hoc Working Group under General Assembly resolution 80/251, co-chaired by Jamaica and Norway. In the first phase, Member States are developing common tools to guide future mandate decisions, including draft concept notes, templates for resolutions and decisions, and standard language for reviewing or retiring mandates. The next phase will assess existing General Assembly mandates for renewal, updating, merging, replacement, or discontinuation, with recommendations expected by end of August 2026. In parallel, the Secretariat is upgrading the mandate registry, building tools to compare changes across resolution texts, creating a central website for mandate-related resources, and reviewing more than 600 reports to identify opportunities to reduce duplication or streamline reporting. Workstream I (Efficiencies) remains stalled in the Fifth Committee amid a deepening liquidity crisis — regular budget collections fell to 76.7% in 2025 with record year-end arrears of $1.57 billion, and as of April 2026 collections stood at 51.4%, leaving cash sufficient only through mid-August. Workstream III (Structural Realignment) advanced with the launch of the 'Progress and Next Steps' report providing one-page summaries of all work packages.

The August 2026 deadline for mandate recommendations creates a near-term decision point that could reshape the UN's programmatic footprint. The liquidity crisis (cash only through mid-August 2026) adds existential urgency — the UN may face a funding cliff before the mandate review completes. For intergenerational equity, the mandate review process determines which youth, future generations, and sustainability programs survive or are retired. signals.title: Article 109 Coalition Advances UN Charter Amendment Pathway as Reform Track Alongside Pact for the Future

The coalition positions Article 109 as a complementary reform track alongside the Pact for the Future and UN80, noting that while the Pact advances implementation within the existing Charter framework, Article 109 addresses the Charter's structural limitations - including Security Council composition, veto powers, and the absence of future generations as a governance principle. signals.why_it_matters: Article 109 represents the constitutional reform track for the UN system - distinct from and complementary to the Pact for the Future's implementation agenda and UN80's administrative reform. signals.title: Hawaii Enacts SB 2401 Creating Regional Shoreline Mitigation Districts for Coordinated Climate Adaptation
signals.summary: On July 8, 2026, Governor Josh Green signed SB 2401 into law as Act 207, establishing a framework for Regional Shoreline Mitigation Districts in Hawaii. The legislation authorizes the creation of special districts that can coordinate and finance shoreline protection, beach restoration, and climate adaptation measures across property boundaries and jurisdictional lines. These districts can levy assessments, issue bonds, and access state funding to implement regional-scale nature-based and engineered solutions to sea-level rise, coastal erosion, and storm surge — moving beyond the current parcel-by-parcel approach that has led to fragmented, often maladaptive armoring. The measure was developed in coordination with the Hawaii Climate Change Mitigation and Adaptation Commission (CCMAC) and the Department of Land and Natural Resources.

Shoreline mitigation districts operationalize the principle that coastal resilience is a collective, long-horizon obligation: today's property owners and taxpayers invest in protection that primarily benefits future residents who will face escalating sea-level rise (Hawaii projects up to 4 feet by 2100). The district model solves the collective-action problem of individualized seawalls that accelerate neighbor erosion, replacing it with a pooled-risk, pooled-investment structure. signals.summary: On May 29, 2025, 22 youth plaintiffs (19 from Montana, lead plaintiff Eva Lighthiser of Missoula, including 10 Held v. Montana veterans) filed Lighthiser v. The district court (Judge Sam Haddon) dismissed the case on October 15, 2025, for lack of standing and political question doctrine, following Ninth Circuit precedent in Juliana v. United States. The Ninth Circuit heard oral arguments April 13, 2026, and on June 2, 2026, a three-judge panel unanimously affirmed dismissal, holding plaintiffs' injuries were 'too speculative' and causation 'mere conjecture.' Our Children's Trust is reviewing Supreme Court certiorari options. The case was filed in Montana because lead plaintiffs are Montana residents and the state's constitutional climate precedent (Held) informed the legal strategy.

The Ninth Circuit's June 2026 affirmation deepens the federal judicial barrier to youth climate claims (paralleling Juliana), creating a stark divergence: Montana state courts enforce youth climate rights (Held affirmed Dec 2024), while federal courts reject them. signals.title: European Commission Adopts First-Ever Strategy on Intergenerational Fairness
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: On 5 March 2026, the European Commission adopted its first-ever Strategy on Intergenerational Fairness (COM(2026) 110 final), fulfilling a commitment in President von der Leyen's 2024-2029 Political Guidelines. The strategy, developed under Commissioner Glenn Micallef (Intergenerational Fairness, Youth, Culture and Sport), establishes a framework for systematic engagement with fair distribution of opportunities and burdens across generations. It introduces an 'intergenerational fairness contract' built on three pillars: fair policymaking (mainstreaming future generations into impact assessments and legislative drafting), fair opportunities (education, skills, housing, labour market entry), and fair places (territorial cohesion, climate resilience, digital access). The strategy commits to an intergenerational fairness check on all major legislative proposals and an annual monitoring report.
signals.why_it_matters: This is the most significant institutional milestone for intergenerational fairness governance in the EU since the creation of the Commissioner portfolio itself. The strategy moves the concept from political rhetoric into the EU's legislative machinery — binding intergenerational fairness checks on all major proposals, annual monitoring, and a cross-cutting framework that spans competitiveness, social policy, climate, and territorial cohesion. No other major jurisdiction has institutionalised intergenerational fairness at this scale in the legislative process. The Council's subsequent preparation of conclusions (ST-8687/26) and the European Economic and Social Committee's opinion process signal multi-institutional embedding. For the platform's mission, this is a flagship signal of intergenerational equity becoming operational governance architecture.

signals.title: Youth Progress Index 2025: Global Opportunity and Rights Stagnate While Basic Needs Rise Across 169 Countries
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: The fourth Youth Progress Index (YPI 2025), published November 2025 by the European Youth Forum with Social Progress Imperative, ranks 169 countries on 61 social and environmental indicators of youth wellbeing over 2015–2024, without using GDP as an input. The world average rose only from about 61.9 to 64.6. Basic Needs improved most (global level ~75.5), Foundations of Wellbeing mid (driven by information and communications +9.4), while Opportunity barely moved (~56.9) and the Rights & Voice component fell roughly four points. North America is the only region with net overall regression, led by an Opportunity drop of about 4.1 points; the United States (−2.1) and Canada (−1.4) appear among the largest national score declines. This edition overlays a rights-based reading of the indicators and calls for a UN Convention on the Rights of Young People plus coordinated global youth-disaggregated data infrastructure. Nuance: YPI measures present youth cohort outcomes as a rights proxy, not future-generations institutions or intergenerational fiscal transfers; some civic indicators are adult-level proxies; authors state it is not a comprehensive rights audit.
signals.why_it_matters: YPI is the largest global youth-wellbeing composite and a measurement template for intergenerational equity debates that often stop at GDP or youth participation rhetoric. The pattern it quantifies — rising survival floors with stagnant opportunity and eroding civic rights — is the structural diagnosis the platform already tracks qualitatively (Naides trust gap; GYPI socio-economic vs civic split). For foresight, it supplies peer-relative (GDP-controlled) performance, component-level alerts, and a beyond-GDP architecture. For GYC framework-building it anchors Layer A–C (present outcomes, agency conditions, material preconditions) while exposing what still must be measured separately: future-generations institutions, fiscal/climate transfers, and participation influence rather than presence. Italy is already piloting YPI methodologies in its 2026 Youth Voluntary Review, so the index is moving from advocacy dataset toward policy tooling.

signals.title: JRC 2025: EU Young Cohorts Stagnate on Income and Lose Homeownership Versus Same-Age Predecessors
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: In December 2025 the Joint Research Centre published Intergenerational fairness in the EU: income and housing dynamics in the context of demographic change (JRC144437). Using Luxembourg Income Study and EU-SILC microdata, the report compares generations at the same age over the life course rather than only cross-sectional age groups. It finds that recent cohorts—especially at younger ages—face stagnant disposable income relative to previous generations at the same age, higher poverty risk and low-pay exposure, rising within-generation inequality, falling homeownership, and higher rental cost overburden (notably in cities), amplified by urban migration of young adults and a sharp rise in single households at ages 25–29. Post-2004 Member States show less pronounced income deterioration. The report was produced to inform the EU Intergenerational Fairness Strategy, Affordable Housing Plan, Anti-Poverty Strategy, and related monitoring tools including the Intergenerational Fairness Index. Nuance: coverage is incomplete for full EU27 on long series; it measures living-cohort material outcomes, not future-generations institutions or climate liability; excluding co-resident young from ownership stats avoids parental bias but understates dependence on parents.
signals.why_it_matters: This is the EU’s clearest official template for measuring intergenerational fairness as same-age cohort outcomes—the method that separates normal life-course gaps from true generational decline. It operationalises the material side of intergenerational equity (income, poverty, housing wealth channel) that youth-rights composites like the Youth Progress Index do not resolve, and it supplies the empirical backbone the Commission’s Intergenerational Fairness Index and Strategy need. For the platform, the same-age cohort rule should become a standing analytical standard in country and fiscal IE work: age cross-sections alone misdiagnose fairness.

signals.title: JRC 2024: EU Life-Fairness Perceptions Fall 51% to 38%, Sharpest Among Young People and Students
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: JRC summary report Fairness, inequality and intergenerational mobility (JRC138713, DOI 10.2760/048970) analyses Eurobarometer Special surveys on Fairness, Inequality and Inter-generational mobility for 2017 (Special 471, n≈26,693) and 2022 (Special 529, n≈26,395) across the EU-27. Agreement that things that happen in life are fair fell from 51% to 38%, with the largest declines among young people and students; perceived equality of opportunity also fell (about 57% to 47%), again steepest for 15–24/students. Concern that income inequality is too high stayed very high (85% to 81%). Redistribution support remains around 77%. Parental education is the strongest predictor of tertiary attainment; more than 40% of respondents underestimate their relative income position, with younger people misperceiving more. signals.title: Intergenerational Foundation 2016: EU28 Fairness Index Deteriorates +5.5 Points as Debt and Youth Unemployment Drive Post-Crisis Loss
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: The Intergenerational Foundation’s European Intergenerational Fairness Index 2016 tracks EU28 fairness 2005–2014 with 13 Eurostat/ESS indicators (debt, youth unemployment, pensions and ageing health costs, housing burden, poverty risk, education spending, tertiary attainment, R&D, GHG, democratic participation, incomes, dependency). Aggregate EU index rose to 105.5 by 2014 (base 2005=100)—a +5.5 deterioration after pre-crisis improvement. Critical polarity: higher score means worse for young people. Government debt was the largest driver; youth unemployment rose roughly 15% to 22% post-crisis. Southern Europe (Greece, Italy, Romania, Cyprus) worst; Eastern Europe often better on debt/youth ratios. Foreword by Laurence Kotlikoff calls for explicit youth and future-citizen impact assessment of all policies. Nuance: age-group snapshot not same-age birth cohorts; pre-2015 data; polarity opposite modern higher=better indices (Portugal IJI, YPI, GYPI).
signals.why_it_matters: Classic EU composite ancestor of Portugal IJI and EU IGF Index debates. Establishes the Layer C–D indicator menu (debt, pensions vs education, youth unemployment, housing, environment) still used in IE measurement. For the platform it is a historical baseline that IE is measurable and was deteriorating in post-crisis Europe, plus a standing polarity-hygiene warning when comparing indices. Kotlikoff’s assessment demand prefigures Youth Check / SOIF toolkit logic. Relationship memory: Vanhuysse IJI (debt-per-child upgrade), JRC cohort method, EU Strategy Index commitment.

signals.title: SOIF–Gulbenkian Framework for Intergenerational Fairness: Institutions, National Dialogue, and Five Unfairness Tests for Policy Assessment
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: School of International Futures and the Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation co-designed a Framework for Intergenerational Fairness (Pilot Report Dec 2020; Specialist Report 2021) with more than 400 experts and citizens in Portugal, built for global adaptation. Fair policies must allow people of all ages to meet needs now and meet present needs without compromising future generations (Brundtland-auditable). The system has three required elements: institutional ownership/legitimacy; national dialogue for a shared future vision; and a policy assessment toolkit applying five unfairness tests ex-ante and ex-post across alternative futures—disadvantage to a life stage; disadvantage to a time period; inequality transmission through time; restriction of future choices; drift from shared future vision. Not a scored country ranking. Authors stress politicians lack long-term distributional information and a constituency for unborn/young non-voters, and that change often requires civil-society pressure. Nuance: process tool, not outcome index; toolkit alone insufficient without institutions and dialogue.
signals.why_it_matters: Best Layer E process framework in the measurement library: how to assess policies for IE, not only rank countries. Complements Portugal IJI (same Gulbenkian lineage, outcome dashboard) and the EU Strategy Youth Check/foresight tools. For platform signals and country briefs it supplies a reusable five-test checklist for why_it_matters and mechanism analysis. signals.title: Vanhuysse 2013 Bertelsmann IJI: OECD Intergenerational Justice via Ecological Footprint, Child Poverty, Debt-per-Child, and Elderly Spending Bias
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: Pieter Vanhuysse’s Intergenerational Justice in Aging Societies (Bertelsmann Stiftung, 2013) builds a synthetic Intergenerational Justice Index for 29 OECD countries at a late-2000s/early-2010s snapshot. Four dimensions: ecological footprint; child poverty (including relative to old-age poverty); public debt per child; and EBiSS—the Elderly Bias Indicator of Social Spending, demography-adjusted. Dual weighting schemes (researcher-imposed and benefit-of-the-doubt). Top cluster included Estonia, Korea, Israel, New Zealand, Hungary and Nordics; bottom included USA, Japan, Italy, Greece and Canada. Debt per child ranged extremely (e.g. Japan hundreds of thousands of dollars per child vs low-debt peers). No OECD country met a ~1.8 gha/cap sustainable footprint benchmark. Core claim: aging is ethically neutral; the policy package is the justice variable. Nuance: cross-sectional snapshot not full cohort life-course accounts; pre-crisis residual timing for some series; ranks are historical structure not live 2026 scores.
signals.why_it_matters: Canonical OECD IE measurement model and still underused Layer D toolkit: debt-per-child beats raw debt/GDP, and EBiSS shows demography does not fully explain pro-elderly spending skew. Foundational citation for later national IE indices (Portugal IJI lineage). For the platform it upgrades scorecard fiscal liability metrics and frames aging as constraint not automatic injustice. Relationship memory: IF 2016 EU menu; Portugal IJI public-finance redesign; JRC same-age income/housing method.

signals.title: Galasso Age-It 2025: European Index of Intergenerational Justice Finds Economic and Political Skew Toward Older Adults, Relational Edge for Young
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: Vincenzo Galasso and Age-It collaborators published An index of intergenerational justice: main concepts and preliminary evidence (Journals of Gerontology Series B, 2025; doi 10.1093/geronb/gbaf192), with a Bocconi/Age-It 2025 report applying the index across 19 EU countries. The snapshot compares younger adults (25–34) with older adults (55–64 labour; 65+ broader) on four dimensions: economic fairness (poverty, unemployment, contracts, wages, housing, financial resilience); access to services/public goods (healthcare, non-pension transfers, environment, safety, digital); relational equality (networks, leisure, discrimination, mental wellbeing); and political equality (interest, voting, party ID, manifesto saliency, parliamentary age composition). Coding: more=better; positive values favor older adults, negative favor younger; three weighting schemes (equal, empirical via life satisfaction, normative). Findings: older adults dominate economic and political dimensions; younger adults dominate relational equality; services mixed; aggregate balance often masks offsetting inequalities (Ireland/Italy lean elderly; Croatia/Lithuania/Slovenia lean young). Age-group not birth-cohort design by deliberate choice. Nuance: living-generation justice, not unborn FG welfare; not the official EU Intergenerational Fairness Index.
signals.why_it_matters: Most recent academic European multi-dimension IE index, bridging generational-accounting politics with measurable age-group fairness across economy, services, relationships and political power. Complements JRC same-age cohort income/housing (method purity) and Vanhuysse/IF (liabilities) by adding relational and political equality into one frame. For GYC it supplies Layer B political under-representation metrics next to GYPI and Layer C–D economic skew evidence for Southern Europe. Relationship memory: Age-It NRRP research; Population Europe policy insights; EU Strategy measurement track.

signals.title: Global Carbon Budget 2025: Fossil CO2 at Record High; Remaining 1.5°C Carbon Budget Virtually Exhausted
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: The Global Carbon Budget 2025 (Global Carbon Project; 20th edition), synthesised in official FAQs and building on the peer-reviewed ESSD carbon-budget accounting series (Friedlingstein et al.), projects fossil CO2 emissions at a record ~38.1 GtCO2 in 2025 (+1.1%), with land-use-change emissions ~4.1 GtCO2. The remaining carbon budget to limit warming to 1.5°C is described as virtually exhausted; at current rates there is roughly a one-in-two chance that about four more years of current CO2 emissions would bring multi-year 1.5°C breach. Remaining budgets for 1.7°C and 2°C are given as ~525 GtCO2 (~12 years) and ~1055 GtCO2 (~25 years) at 2025 emissions levels. Climate change is already weakening land and ocean sinks (~8% of atmospheric CO2 rise since 1960 attributed to sink weakening). 35 countries cut emissions over 2015–2024 while growing GDP. Novel CDR methods remain negligible vs fossil emissions. Nuance: budgets depend on probability choices and non-CO2 pathways; GCB is scientific accounting not a justice composite; equity of budget allocation across countries/cohorts is a policy layer on top of the physical stock.
signals.why_it_matters: Remaining carbon budget is the core Layer D climate-stock metric for intergenerational equity: cumulative CO2 left is what present generations can still emit without foreclosing safe climate for younger and unborn cohorts. GCB is the operational standard updating IPCC AR6 remaining-budget figures annually and should anchor scorecard climate-liability signals alongside Portugal IJI GHG paths and Vanhuysse ecological footprint. Relationship memory: Paris Agreement NDC/stocktake cycle; youth climate litigation; EU IGF environmental measurement debates.

signals.title: Naides / UNU-CPR: Intergenerational Trust Gap Framework — Recognition, Representation, Redistribution as Governance Test of the Era
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: Shai Naides (Global Policy Manager for Intergenerational Governance and Participation, UNICEF Innocenti), published via UNU Centre for Policy Research, diagnoses an intergenerational trust gap: when authority operates in short electoral/budget cycles while exposure accumulates over decades, younger cohorts experience governance as done to them not with them. Nearly half the world is under 30 while leadership stays older; OECD and trust surveys show eroded youth confidence and widespread belief children will be worse off than parents. Core distinction: participation volume is widespread (youth councils, consultations) but participation agency is rare—presence without decision-shaping power erodes legitimacy. Three interdependent conditions for meaningful participation: Recognition (youth perspectives treated as relevant to long-term risk), Representation (embedded decision pathways not parallel consultative spaces), and Redistribution (material conditions—education, work, security—that enable participation). Youth act as informal early-warning sensors when legitimacy fractures; where channels fail, willingness for more disruptive action rises. Closing claim: intergenerational governance is a key governance test of this era. Nuance: analytic essay, not a scored index; cites Edelman, OECD, ILO, IPU, CFR as evidence base.
signals.why_it_matters: Primary Layer B/F theory frame for the platform: agency over presence, material preconditions for voice, and trust/legitimacy as early-warning. Maps directly onto GYPI (structures), YPI Opportunity lag, JRC fairness collapse, and protest-threshold signals already in the database. For scorecard and thematic synthesis it supplies the Recognition–Representation–Redistribution checklist and the barrier-not-apathy interpretive rule. Relationship memory: already referenced across dozens of IE signals; this record makes the primary source itself a first-class intel object.

signals.title: Fiji Youth Councils Urge Constitutional Youth Seats, Intergenerational Responsibility and Climate Justice
signals.summary: In early July 2026 submissions to Fiji's Constitution Review Commission, the National Youth Council of Fiji, Provincial Youth Forum and Youth Assemblies of Fiji called for four dedicated youth seats in Parliament and for Chapter 1 of the Constitution to enshrine intergenerational responsibility—requiring the State to consider the rights, welfare and future security of children, young people and future generations in major public decisions. Distinct from the parallel FICA debt-stewardship submission, it treats young people as present rights-holders and seeks hard institutional seats rather than consultative soft power. If any elements enter the review draft, Fiji would join a small set of jurisdictions experimenting with constitutional intergenerational equity language beyond environmental preambles.

For foresight, it reinforces a 2026 pattern of OECD surveys (also Norway, Korea) treating ageing costs as intergenerational fairness problems rather than pure technocratic finance.

The recurring youth parliament format brings young people into structured deliberation on water policy, climate-linked hydrology and cross-border basin management, producing recommendations aimed at European and national water institutions.
signals.why_it_matters: Water governance is a classic intergenerational commons problem—allocation today locks in drought, flood and ecosystem outcomes for later cohorts. A dedicated European youth parliament focused on watersheds is a concrete participation channel beyond one-off climate COPs, testing whether youth deliberative institutions can influence river-basin and EU water acquis implementation. September outcomes (recommendations, institutional uptake) are the next checkpoint.

signals.title: Wales Future Generations Commissioner Publishes Statutory 2025 Report With 38 Recommendations Ahead of Senedd Election
signals.summary: Wales' Future Generations Commissioner Derek Walker published the statutory Future Generations Report 2025 on 29 April 2025, the five-yearly assessment required by the Well-being of Future Generations (Wales) Act 2015. The report makes 38 recommendations across seven missions, including ending short-term fixes, ringfenced prevention funding, a Real Living Wage commitment, a national food resilience plan, and a review to strengthen the Act itself. It serves as advice to the next Senedd after the 2026 election and calls for the Act's scope to be expanded to additional public bodies.
signals.why_it_matters: This is the most comprehensive assessment of Wales' world-leading future generations legislation since its implementation, providing the clearest evidence yet of what a statutory future-generations institution produces in practice. The Commissioner's call to 'review and strengthen the WFG Act' signals that even the gold-standard model requires evolution. The emphasis on prevention spending and wellbeing economy offers concrete policy levers for other jurisdictions considering similar legislation, including Scotland, Australia, Ireland, and the EU.

signals.title: Loss and Damage Fund Board Warns of Capital Depletion by 2027 as Only $456M of $822M Pledged Is Paid
signals.summary: The FRLD Executive Director warned the Board at its 8th meeting in Livingstone, Zambia that the Fund faces liquidity issues by end of 2027, with only $456M of $822M pledged actually paid into the trust fund. signals.title: Ninth Circuit Dismisses Lighthiser v. Trump Youth Climate Challenge to Energy Executive Orders on Standing Grounds
signals.summary: The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals dismissed Lighthiser v. Trump, a lawsuit by 22 young Americans challenging Trump executive orders to expand fossil fuel development. The court ruled the youth lacked standing because their climate injuries bore too tenuous a connection to the executive orders, and that granting the requested injunction would constitute impermissible judicial supervision of executive energy policy. Ten of the plaintiffs had previously prevailed in the landmark Held v. Montana case.
signals.why_it_matters: The ruling illustrates continuing judicial barriers youth plaintiffs face in federal court despite establishing overwhelming evidence of climate harm. The decision reinforces that separation-of-powers doctrines can block youth climate cases even when plaintiffs demonstrate concrete injuries, highlighting the gap between constitutional rights rhetoric and judicial remedies in US federal courts. The involvement of Held v. Montana veterans makes this a direct test of whether state-level climate precedent translates to federal forums.

signals.title: Wisconsin Youth Appeal Dunn v. PSC Dismissal on Constitutional and Public Trust Grounds
signals.summary: Fifteen Wisconsin youth filed Dunn v. Wisconsin Public Service Commission challenging state laws that limit the PSC from considering air pollution when approving fossil fuel plants. The Dane County Circuit Court dismissed on political question grounds in April 2026. The youth plaintiffs appealed in May 2026, arguing the laws violate their constitutional rights to life, liberty, and the public trust doctrine protecting navigable waters for present and future generations. Indigenous youth plaintiffs added claims about threats to traditional lifeways including harvesting wild rice and maple sugar.
signals.why_it_matters: The case raises novel legal questions about whether statutes that structurally exclude climate considerations from regulatory decision-making violate state constitutional rights. The appeal tests whether state courts will enforce intergenerational public trust obligations against legislative limitations on agency authority. The Indigenous youth claims add a dimension of cultural and intergenerational heritage rights not typically present in youth climate litigation.

signals.title: Utah Supreme Court Dismisses Youth Climate Lawsuit Natalie v. State for Lack of Redressability
signals.summary: The Utah Supreme Court dismissed a youth climate lawsuit brought by seven Utahns aged 9-18 challenging state statutory provisions and government conduct promoting fossil fuel development. The Court held that declaring challenged provisions unconstitutional would not redress plaintiffs' injuries because it would not require the government to curb fossil fuel development, and that challenges to government conduct were not tied to specific concrete actions, making them non-justiciable.
signals.why_it_matters: The ruling demonstrates that even when youth plaintiffs can show climate harm, redressability remains a critical barrier when the causal chain between state law and emissions is diffuse. The decision adds to growing case law across US states where courts express sympathy but dismiss youth climate cases on justiciability grounds, while the dismissal was without prejudice, preserving potential for reformulated claims.

signals.title: Swedish Supreme Court Dismisses Aurora Youth Climate Case but Opens Pathway for Association-Led Claims
signals.summary: The Swedish Supreme Court dismissed the Aurora case brought by over 600 young Swedes seeking stronger climate action under the European Convention on Human Rights. The Court ruled individual plaintiffs lacked standing under ECtHR KlimaSeniorinnen criteria, but explicitly left the door open for climate cases brought by qualified associations seeking declarations of rights violations rather than specific policy orders. The case was remitted to district court for possible continuation as an association claim.

The distinction between permissible declarations of rights violations and impermissible orders for specific government action will influence climate litigation strategy throughout the Council of Europe, creating both barriers and pathways for future youth climate cases.

signals.summary: DWP published version 3 of the 2026 to 2027 apprenticeship funding rules on 29 July 2026, applying to starts from 1 August 2026 to 31 July 2027 under the Growth and Skills Levy. signals.title: EU AI Act Reaches Full Application of Core Obligations on 2 August 2026 Amid Omnibus High-Risk Stagger
signals.summary: On 20 July 2026 the Commission adopted Guidelines on implementing Article 50 transparency obligations of the AI Act (C(2026) 5054), 13 days before those obligations applied on 2 August 2026. The guidelines are a distinct implementation instrument, not a restatement of the already-ingested full-application timeline. For interactive AI (Art. 50(1)), providers must take account of children and other vulnerable groups whenever a system is intended or reasonably likely to interact with the public: notifications must be child-friendly, age-appropriate, easy to understand and accessible, including for children with disabilities; terms-and-conditions-only disclosures are insufficient. Periodic reminders are flagged as necessary for children, for sustained immersive use with addiction-like or emotional-dependency risk (explicitly including AI companions), and for health/legal/financial advice. Deployers of emotion-recognition and biometric-categorisation systems must inform everyone exposed, including children (Art. 50(3)). Deep-fake 'false appearance' assessments must consider child audiences with lower AI literacy. Horizontal Art. 50(5) rules require clear, distinguishable, first-interaction information that children can actually perceive. Fines can reach €15 million or 3% of worldwide turnover; national market-surveillance authorities lead enforcement.
signals.why_it_matters: This is the sharpest near-term binding AI governance lock-in for the New Alignment vision's Shift 2: institutions must shape systems in real time, not after the fact. signals.title: ACT Abolishes Stamp Duty for All First Home Buyers From 1 July 2026 as Generational Housing Tax Reform
signals.summary: In the 2026-27 ACT Budget (released 10 June 2026), the Territory becomes the first Australian jurisdiction to abolish stamp duty for all first home buyers from 1 July 2026. Exemptions also expand for pensioners, eligible NDIS participants, and buyers who have not owned property in the previous five years. Parallel measures remove stamp duty on new unit-titled owner-occupier purchases (including turn-key units), continue off-the-plan concessions, and cut Lease Variation Charges for 'missing middle' developments. Treasurer Chris Steel explicitly frames the package as complementing federal housing-tax reforms to support younger generations into ownership; Chief Minister Andrew Barr ties it to a long-term tax-reform program that removes upfront barriers for the next generation.
signals.why_it_matters: This is a concrete operationalisation of intergenerational housing equity on the buyer side of the tax system: eliminating a transaction tax that hits cash-constrained first-time (often younger) buyers hardest, while ACT's broader reform path has shifted revenue toward recurrent land-based charges. It pairs first-home relief with downsizing relief for older owners, making housing-stock turnover an explicit intergenerational mechanism rather than only a supply slogan.

signals.title: Alaska Governor Files HJR 30 to Constitutionalize Permanent Fund 5% POMV Draw and Automatic 50% Dividend
signals.summary: On 23 January 2026, House Rules by request of the Governor introduced HJR 30 (companion SJR 23), a proposed Alaska constitutional amendment on the Permanent Fund. The filed text would keep at least 25% of mineral revenues in the fund, cap annual withdrawals at 5% of a five-year average market-value (POMV) formula, require that 50% of the authorized withdrawal be paid automatically as dividends to eligible residents without appropriation, allow the remainder for government operations, fold the Earnings Reserve Account into principal by 30 June 2027, and place the amendments before voters at the next general election. As of the legislative journal, the measure was referred to House Finance and had not passed. Governor Dunleavy framed the package as permanently protecting the PFD after Wielechowski held that dividends must compete annually for appropriation.
signals.why_it_matters: Alaska’s Permanent Fund is the United States’ flagship nonrenewable-resource trust for future generations, yet the corpus currently tracks Montana/Hawaii trust and climate signals far more densely than Alaska fiscal design. Constitutionalizing a POMV spending rule plus an automatic 50/50 dividend–government split would lock in a durable intergenerational fiscal regime—and create a live tension between present per-capita consumption (PFD) and long-term corpus preservation that other state permanent funds (Minnesota school fund, New Mexico LGPF, North Dakota Legacy Fund) also face.

signals.title: Alaska Supreme Court Hears Sagoonick II Youth Challenge to State-Mandated Alaska LNG Project
signals.summary: On 4 March 2026, eight youth plaintiffs (ages 11–22), including Alaska Native youth, argued before the Alaska Supreme Court in Sagoonick v. State of Alaska II that statutes requiring the Alaska Gasline Development Corporation to advance the Alaska LNG Project violate their state constitutional due process and public-trust rights, including a claimed right to a climate system that sustains human life. The Anchorage Superior Court dismissed the case in March 2025 as a non-justiciable political question; plaintiffs seek reversal and remand for trial, arguing the North Slope-to-export LNG package would roughly triple Alaska greenhouse-gas emissions for decades. Justices pressed counsel on the scope of judicial review and how the case differs from the earlier Sagoonick I dismissal. A decision remains pending.
signals.why_it_matters: This is a live Held-era state supreme court test outside Montana and Hawaii: whether Alaska courts will treat a fossil megaproject mandate as constitutionally reviewable rather than a political question. An affirmance would deepen the US pattern of state youth climate dismissals (Utah Natalie R., Wisconsin Dunn, Florida Reynolds); a reversal would reopen merits litigation against one of the largest proposed US fossil export projects and reinforce Article VIII public-trust framing for future generations.
