signals.title: Cambodia Ministry of Environment Posts Environmental Diplomacy Strategy 2026–2030 After 6 July Launch
signals.summary: The Ministry of Environment of Cambodia’s official homepage, fetched 16 August 2026, lists as a current download ‘Cambodia's Environmental Diplomacy Strategy 2026 - 2030’ and the Khmer counterpart ‘យុទ្ធសាស្រ្ដការទូតបរិស្ថានកម្ពុជា ឆ្នាំ២០២៦ - ២០៣០’, both with last update Monday 6 July 2026. That date matches the ministry launch chaired by Environment Minister Eang Sophalleth, attended by Senate and National Assembly members, other ministries and UNDP. Phnom Penh Post (7 July 2026), attributing photos to the environment ministry, quotes the minister that the strategy is a shared commitment to safeguard the environment for present and future generations and sets three pillars: (1) climate mitigation, adaptation and governance, including forests, clean energy, climate-smart agriculture, green investment, community preparedness and climate finance; (2) ecosystem conservation, protected-area enforcement and forest restoration; (3) pollution control for air, land and water, wastewater, recycling and waste-to-energy. The document is a new 2026–2030 external-engagement framework, not a reprint of the August 2025 NDC 3.0 already in the corpus. The PDF binary linked from the homepage was not retrieved as a standalone file URL in this scan.
signals.why_it_matters: Cambodia’s only ingested signal is NDC 3.0 (August 2025). CEDS 2026–2030 is the ministry’s five-year script for how a highly climate-vulnerable LDC will bargain for climate finance, forest and pollution cooperation while claiming carbon neutrality by 2050. The intergenerational mechanism is an official diplomacy strategy that names present and future generations as the constituency for climate, ecosystem and pollution pillars—shaping what finance and rules later Cambodian cohorts inherit in regional and UNFCCC rooms.

signals.title: Canada Enacts National School Food Program Act, Locking Long-Term Federal Funding for Child Meals
signals.summary: On 26 March 2026 Bill C-15 (Budget Implementation Act, 2025, No. 1) received Royal Assent and enacted the National School Food Program Act as section 599 of chapter 3 of the Statutes of Canada, 2026, in force on assent. The Act’s vision is that all children and youth in Canada have access to nutritious food at school in an inclusive, non-stigmatizing setting that strengthens connections with local food systems, the environment and culture. It commits the Government of Canada to maintaining long-term funding through agreements with provinces, territories or Indigenous governing bodies, guided by accessibility, health promotion, inclusivity, flexibility, sustainability and accountability, and requires an annual report tabled in Parliament. Finance Canada’s 26 March release states the Act helps provide meals for up to 400,000 more children annually. ESDC’s 27 May 2026 release records that Budget 2025 also committed $216.6 million per year from 2029–30 to make the programme permanent, and that all provinces and territories had signed bilateral agreements by 10 March 2025. The Justice Laws full text was last modified 6 August 2026.
signals.why_it_matters: School meals convert a child’s daily nutrition and attendance into a statutory federal funding duty rather than a time-limited budget line, so later cohorts keep the meal even when a future cabinet would rather cut discretionary spending. Local-sourcing language ties today’s public procurement to family-farm and Indigenous food systems that the next generation will inherit, while the CRC and SDG recitals make child food access a rights-and-future-generations obligation, not charity.

signals.title: Costa Rica Enacts Law 10896 Reforming Youth Committees under the General Young Persons Act
signals.summary: On 8 June 2026 Costa Rica published Legislative Decree 10896 (file 23.594) in Alcance 71 to La Gaceta No. 104, reforming the second paragraph of Article 24 of Law 8261 (Ley General de la Persona Joven, 2 May 2002) to guarantee that municipal and district youth committees actually exist and function. The Assembly’s Comisión Legislativa Plena Primera and plenary approved the reform on 25 March 2026; President Laura Fernández Delgado executed it on 12 May 2026 with the Ministers of Culture and Youth and of Interior. Each municipality and district council must constitute its comité de la persona joven in October–November of even years, with functions starting 1 January of the following odd year. If force majeure, duly justified to the Consejo de la Persona Joven, blocks that window, an extraordinary call may run through December of the even year and January of the odd year so the committee can still serve the rest of the term. The law takes effect on publication.
signals.why_it_matters: Costa Rica’s youth committees are the local seats through which people under 35 feed municipal agendas; empty or late-formed committees leave later cohorts without a standing voice in local budgets and climate/risk plans. The reform converts a calendar duty into a backstop: if a municipality misses the even-year window, the national youth council can still force constitution rather than leaving a two-year vacancy. Mechanism: statutory amendment of Law 8261 Art. 24 plus an extraordinary-call path supervised by the Consejo de la Persona Joven, so local youth representation is not optional between election cycles.

signals.title: Costa Rica Gazettes Law 10954 Approving a USD 370 Million Climate-Resilient Reconstruction Loan
signals.summary: On 20 May 2026 Costa Rica published Legislative Decree 10954 (file 24.761) approving Financing Agreement 9653-CR with IBRD, plus GCFF trust fund TF0C4693-CR, for the Programa de Reconstrucción y Desarrollo Territorial Resiliente al Clima. The package is USD 370 million: a USD 350 million IBRD loan and a USD 20 million GCFF concessional slice. The Assembly approved the law on 11 May 2026; President Fernández executed it on 15 May 2026. The CNE is the executing agency and must form a programme unit reporting to its Executive Directorate. The project objective, copied into the gazetted Spanish translation of Annex 1, is to increase access to disaster- and climate-resilient infrastructure and services in selected regions. Part 1 finances grey/green flood works, slope stabilisation and critical road/bridge reconstruction; Part 2 finances emergency warehouses, multi-purpose shelters, a new CNE headquarters/emergency operations centre, basin-scale early-warning systems, municipal emergency-committee capacity, an inclusive community-recovery policy, and gender-specific design in critical infrastructure; Part 3 covers project management, climate-indicator monitoring and grievance mechanisms. Disbursements for Part 1 go to the Fondo Nacional de Emergencias; Parts 2–3 to CNE accounts. A World Bank letter of 2 March 2026 had reinstated the 2024 financing agreement after it lapsed on 30 January 2026 and extended effectiveness to 30 July 2026; the May gazette is the domestic statute that makes that package Costa Rican law.
signals.why_it_matters: Without a statutory appropriation, residual flood and slope risk stays on the next cohort as lost schools, roads and delayed warning. Law 10954 converts a lapsed 2024 World Bank package into domestic law so CNE can build climate-resilient works and early-warning systems rather than refinancing disaster losses through the ordinary budget. Mechanism: legislative approval of IBRD loan 9653-CR plus a GCFF concessional sleeve, executed by CNE, with a PDO that names climate-resilient infrastructure and services as the public good later cohorts inherit.

signals.title: Dominican Republic Registers NDC 3.0 with a 28–32% GHG Cut and Child-and-Youth Cross-Cutting Measures
signals.summary: On 9 June 2026 the UNFCCC NDC registry marked Dominican Republic NDC 3.0 (NDC 3.0 RD-2025) active and posted the official Spanish PDF. Versus a 2022-based BAU path the pledge cuts GHG 28% by 2030 (14,732.1 kt CO2eq) and 32% by 2035 (18,349.32 kt CO2eq). Of the 2030 cut, 8.5% is unconditional on national resources and 19.5% is conditional on external finance, technology and capacity; NDC 2.0 (2020) had been 27% by 2030 (7% unconditional / 20% conditional). Mitigation needs an estimated USD 11,468 million across 26 PAMs in energy, IPPU, agriculture, LULUCF and waste; adaptation adds 41 measures and 155 targets in seven sectors at about USD 12,251 million (ministry launch: combined envelope above USD 23,719 million). The text newly names primera infancia, niñez and adolescencia alongside youth, gender, disability, just transition and ACE as cross-cutting elements, cites LCOY-RD and the 2025 CLAC-RD child-rights study, and lists INAIPI, CONANI and the Ministry of Youth among implementation actors. MMARN, CNCCMC and the Ministry of Finance and Economy ran the update with IDB finance. The Presidency announced readiness to deposit on 29 April 2026; MMARN held the public launch on 25 June 2026 during the first Climate Finance Week. A climate-framework statute is still not in Congress.
signals.why_it_matters: As a small-island developing state, the Dominican Republic’s residual cyclone, drought and coastal-erosion risk falls on children who will live with 2035 infrastructure and fiscal space. Registering NDC 3.0 locks a 2026–2035 emissions path, a dated finance envelope, and—unlike NDC 2.0—explicit first-childhood and youth implementation actors, so today’s energy, water and coastal choices are no longer only an adult mitigation account. Mechanism: a Paris Agreement NDC 3.0 on the UNFCCC registry, with ACE and child/youth transversal measures, still without a domestic climate law.

signals.title: Ecuador Publishes ARTTRM Rule Enabling Paris Article 6 International Carbon Transfers
signals.summary: Acuerdo Ministerial MAE-MAE-2026-0055-AM, signed 30 April 2026 by Minister Inés María Manzano Díaz and published in Registro Oficial Año II Primer Suplemento No. 289 of 21 May 2026, issues the Norma Técnica para la Autorización, Registro, Trazabilidad y Transferencia de Resultados de Mitigación (ARTTRM). Final provision four brings it into force on gazette publication. Article 1 creates the legal regime for authorising, registering, tracing, accounting, internationally transferring, using, retiring, revoking, cancelling and reporting mitigation outcomes generated in Ecuador, implements Paris Article 6.2 cooperative approaches, and positions Ecuador as host under Article 6.4, operationalising the pending ‘Vía 3’ left by Acuerdo Ministerial MAATE-2023-053. Article 7 requires accounting consistency with the Second NDC (2026–2035). The ministry’s 29 May 2026 bulletin (No. 273) states the rule is now in force for energy, industry, waste and agriculture, with World Bank, GGGI and AECID support. This is distinct from the already ingested ANII 2025–2029 agenda, Yasuní ITT compliance suit, and Waorani FPIC judgment.
signals.why_it_matters: Article 6 transfers decide whether Ecuador’s remaining carbon budget is used at home for the 2026–2035 NDC or sold abroad as internationally transferred mitigation outcomes. That is an intergenerational allocation: today’s fiscal and project revenues versus the mitigation still available to later cohorts, under a sovereign authorisation and corresponding-adjustment lock that the 2023 compensation scheme had left unwritten.

signals.title: Estonia Cabinet Approves Nature Restoration Plan Principles and Targets End-2026 Commission Filing After 1 September Deadline
signals.summary: On 21 May 2026 Estonia's Government Cabinet approved principles for drafting the national nature restoration plan (looduse taastamise kava) under Regulation (EU) 2024/1991. The Climate Ministry page, last updated 10 July 2026, publishes the Cabinet mandate PDF and states the final version is due at the end of 2026. The mandate itself records that Member States must submit a draft to the Commission by 1 September 2026, then explicitly says Estonia will file its draft by the end of 2026 after broad engagement, and asks the energy and climate minister to prepare a protocol decision approving the draft for the Commission by 31 December 2026. Principles include meeting the Regulation at the minimum necessary level, preferring existing programmes, applying new private-land measures outside protected areas on a voluntary basis (except urban ecosystems and river connectivity), preferring state land, and staging measures to the budget. A public involvement seminar on 14 May 2026 opened expert-group measure proposals; a 15 May ministry news item said Estonia aims to submit the plan to the Commission by year-end.
signals.why_it_matters: Estonia is locking a 2030-2050 restoration timetable while openly slipping the 1 September 2026 draft-submission date and capping private-land duties. Mechanism: a Cabinet-approved NRP mandate that delays Commission filing to 31 December 2026 and makes most new private-land restoration voluntary shifts restoration costs and ecological deficit onto later cohorts and onto public land, so younger generations inherit both a later start and a narrower privately financed restoration base.

signals.title: Ethiopia Council of Ministers Adopts a National Energy Policy for Immediate Implementation Under the Green Economy Strategy
signals.summary: On 26 May 2026 Ethiopia’s Council of Ministers adopted a draft National Energy Policy and decreed its immediate implementation from the date of adoption. The official ENA sitting report states the policy is harmonised with the Homegrown Economic Reform, the Ten-Year Development Plan, the Green Economy Strategy and the Sustainable Development Goals, and is framed as a framework to harness national energy resources so as to guarantee a sustainable, reliable, secure, cost-effective and competitive supply while maximising benefits for all citizens. The same sitting referred the carbon-market bill, tax-administration amendment, statistics bill, food-system-and-nutrition bill and agricultural-business-company bill to the House, and adopted a National Policy on Women’s Empowerment and Gender Equality for immediate implementation. No standalone energy-policy PDF or Negarit Gazette instrument was retrieved in this scan.

signals.title: Ethiopia House Enacts Carbon Market Proclamation No. 1436/2018 to Operationalise the 2025–2035 Strategy
signals.summary: On 30 June 2026, at its 29th regular session, Ethiopia’s House of People’s Representatives ratified the Ethiopian Carbon Market Proclamation (No. 1436/2018, Ethiopian calendar) by majority vote with one abstention. The statute is the legal architecture for the National Carbon Market Strategy 2025–2035: it consolidates previously fragmented carbon-trading rules, regulates carbon credits, and is designed to attract green investment, enable technology transfer, and set transparent revenue-sharing among government, developers, local communities and other stakeholders. Standing Committee on Plan, Budget and Finance chair Desalegn Wedaje told the House the proclamation creates the institutional mechanisms needed to implement treaties Ethiopia has ratified, including the Paris Agreement and its greenhouse-gas pledges. The Council of Ministers had unanimously approved the draft and referred it to the House on 26 May 2026, with the same sitting stressing community and environmental safeguards at host sites. As of 16 August 2026 the Federal Negarit Gazette text was not retrieved; hopr.gov.et still listed the draft (የካርቦን ገበያ ረቂቅ አዋጅ) among drafted laws dated 16 June 2026.
signals.why_it_matters: Ethiopia’s NDC 3.0 (registered 26 September 2025) already locks a 70.3% cut versus revised BAU by 2035 and a USD 106 billion finance envelope that later cohorts will inherit. Without a statute, Article 6 credits and community revenue shares remained discretionary, so today’s land, forest and energy projects could transfer climate rent away from the generation that will live with residual emissions and lost livelihoods. Mechanism: House enactment of Proclamation 1436/2018 creating a unified carbon-market law with named revenue-sharing and host-community safeguards, still pending Negarit Gazette promulgation.

signals.title: Georgia Inserts GHG Emission Authorisation and Annual Verified MRV into the Environmental Protection Law (Law 1525 of 28 April 2026)
signals.summary: Law of Georgia No. 1525-Vმს-XIმპ of 28 April 2026, published on matsne.gov.ge on 1 May 2026, amends the 1996 Law on Environmental Protection. The official English consolidated text inserts Article 51-1 (Authorisation of greenhouse gas emissions) and Article 51-2 (Monitoring, reporting and verification of greenhouse gas emissions). Operators of activities listed by government ordinance must obtain an individual GHG-emissions authorisation from the National Environmental Agency (Civil Aviation Agency for aviation), including a monitoring-and-reporting plan; authorisation is granted for an indefinite period and is transferable. Article 51-2 requires annual GHG reports by 31 March, verified by an accredited verifier, with the granting body publishing verified reports on the environmental information portal within five business days. Matsne flags a transitional provision; at least Article 51-1(14) (portal publication of transfer acts) and the verifier definition become effective from 1 January 2028. Distinct from Ordinance 122 / NDC 3.0 (the international pledge) and from the 2023 Industrial Emissions Law whose integrated-permit articles enter force on 1 September 2026: this is the first gazetted operator-level GHG authorisation and verified annual MRV inside the Environmental Protection Law.
signals.why_it_matters: Without operator-level GHG permits and verified annual reports, NDC 3.0 targets remain a paper pledge while today’s emitters pass the residual carbon stock to later Georgian cohorts. Mechanism: a 28 April 2026 statute, published 1 May 2026, that writes indefinite GHG authorisation, monitoring plans, accredited verification and public MRV into primary environmental law, with specified clauses commencing 1 January 2028.

signals.title: Germany Transposes the EU Right-to-Repair Directive into the Civil Code from 31 July 2026
signals.summary: The Gesetz zur Umsetzung der Richtlinie (EU) 2024/1799 zur Förderung der Reparatur von Waren sowie zur Verbesserung der Verfügbarkeit von Vorsorgeverfügungen was signed on 16 July 2026 (Steinmeier / Merz / Hubig) and promulgated as BGBl. 2026 I Nr. 212 on 22 July 2026. Article 1 inserts BGB Untertitel 4 “Reparaturverpflichtung des Herstellers” (§§ 479a–479g): for Annex II goods bought by consumers outside seller-liability, manufacturers must repair within a reasonable time, offer spare parts and tools at non-deterrent prices, publish typical repair prices, and must not use hardware or software that impedes independent repair (including used, compatible or 3-D-printed parts) unless justified by IP or product safety. Choosing repair once extends the original defect-claim limitation period by 12 months (§ 475e(5)). EGBGB Article 229 § 72 applies the new sales-contract rules only to contracts concluded on or after 31 July 2026. The Act entered into force the day after promulgation, except Central Precaution Register amendments on 1 October 2026. Distinct from already-ingested EU Circular Economy Act consultations and youth-check events; this is a Member State transposition statute.
signals.why_it_matters: Throwaway electronics and appliances shift material and waste costs onto the next users of the same city. A manufacturer duty to repair, with spare parts at non-deterrent prices and a 12-month guarantee bonus for choosing repair, keeps goods in use so today’s consumption does not lock later cohorts into replacement demand and landfill. Germany’s BGB text is the first large-Member-State gazette implementation of Directive 2024/1799’s 31 July 2026 application date.

Tender CR_0 (third CfP, official deadline 21 August 2026 23:59 CEST) is a consultancy to design a CDRFI implementation-support structure for SUGESE and a financial-sustainability strategy for Global Shield activities. Tender CR_A1 (second CfP, official deadline 28 August 2026) is a feasibility study for an open-access national climate-and-disaster risk data platform; research institutions, academia, data/risk modellers and public or private entities, including local partners, are invited. Submissions go through the DTVP procurement portal. Neither call appears in signals-db.json or prior-wave opportunity files.

signals.title: Jordan Environment Ministry Launches 2026–2029 Strategy for Climate Action and Green Growth
signals.summary: On 14 July 2026 Jordan’s Ministry of Environment held a high-level event, ‘Green Growth in Jordan: The Way Forward,’ to review the Sustainable Environment driver of the second executive programme of the Economic Modernization Vision. Minister Ayman Suleiman framed the driver as protecting natural resources, strengthening climate resilience and supporting a low-emission green economy. At the close, Secretary-General Omar Arabiyat launched the ministry’s 2026–2029 strategy to guide the next four years, focused on strengthening climate action, accelerating green growth, protecting natural resources and biodiversity, and developing environmental governance, aligned with the EMV, the Public Sector Modernization Roadmap, and Jordan’s national and international environment commitments. A panel with the Prime Ministry Government Achievement Unit, GIZ GAIN and UNDP discussed driver-target progress. As of 16 August 2026 the ministry’s Strategic Plan page still lists the 2023–2025 strategy as the latest downloadable file (last site update 24 February 2026); no 2026–2029 PDF was retrieved on moenv.gov.jo.
signals.why_it_matters: Jordan’s water-energy-food stress already shifts drought, fiscal and climate-adaptation costs onto younger cohorts. A four-year ministry strategy that names climate action and environmental governance as the operating frame for 2026–2029 is the attempt to lock EMV green-transition language into the institution that writes environmental legislation and NDC follow-through, rather than leaving the 2023–2025 plan to lapse without a successor. Mechanism: Secretary-General launch of the Ministry of Environment 2026–2029 strategy at an official Petra-reported sitting, still pending a posted instrument on moenv.gov.jo. signals.title: Kenya Launches NextGen.Ke, a Ksh 2 Billion Stipend Internship Pathway for 30,000 Youth
signals.summary: On 24 July 2026 at State House, Nairobi, President William Ruto launched the NextGen.Ke Youth Employment Programme, a Government of Kenya–UNDP–Kenya Private Sector Alliance (KEPSA) internship scheme, and signed into action a Ksh 2 billion Treasury allocation. The programme places graduates in stipend-supported private-sector internships of up to six months with on-the-job training and mentorship. It is designed to support 30,000 young Kenyans over three years, with a government target to scale to 100,000; 22 companies had already taken 500 interns in the first cohort. UNDP provided USD 1.35 million in catalytic funding. Treasury CS John Mbadi framed the investment as economic, citing that about 75% of Kenyans are under 35. The President announced planned tax-relief incentives for employers who host interns. Official presidency speeches index lists the launch speech on 24 July 2026. Distinct from the already-ingested 23 June 2026 NYOTA cooperative-savings disbursement.
signals.why_it_matters: Kenya’s labour market absorbs only about a quarter of the million young people who enter it each year, so a missing first job becomes lifetime scarring. NextGen.Ke uses public money to buy a first workplace spell—stipend, mentor, private-sector desk—so this cohort can convert a certificate into experience before that window closes, rather than leaving the cost of youth joblessness on later taxpayers and on the next, larger youth bulge.

signals.title: Lao PDR Launches National Food-Systems Action Plan 2025–2030 After Agriculture–Environment Ministry Merger
signals.summary: On 2 March 2026 in Vientiane the Government of Lao PDR launched its National Action Plan on Transition toward Sustainable Food Systems Transformation (2025–2030), chaired by Minister Linkham Douangsavanh of the merged Ministry of Agriculture and Environment (MAE), with the UN Resident Coordinator, FAO and ADB. State news agency KPL (3 March) records seven core programmes: food security and nutrition; commercial agricultural and forestry production; forest management; land allocation; water resources; environmental protection; and rural development and poverty reduction. Consultations included government, partners, farmers, youth and women, aligned with the 10th National Socio-Economic Development Plan. FAO’s official country release the same day states 20 strategic action areas and 62 priority milestones, frames the plan as a response to a ‘5F’ food-feed-fuel-fertilizer-finance crisis, and quotes the minister that merging Agriculture and Forestry with Natural Resources and Environment allows integrated planning of land, water, biodiversity and climate for the first time. Implementation finance cited by FAO includes a USD 4.5 million UN Joint Programme (seven agencies) in Luang Prabang and Oudomxay and USD 33 million ADB co-financing. KPL closes with a government pledge of a sustainable environment for coming generations.

Food, forest and climate risk in the Mekong headwaters is an intergenerational asset problem: degraded soils, forests and nutrition today lock in later health and livelihood losses. signals.title: Lao PDR Opens Southeast Asia’s First Sovereign Anticipatory Drought-Insurance Pilot via SEADRIF
signals.summary: On 30 May 2026 Lao state news agency KPL reported that SEADRIF Insurance Company and FAO launched an anticipatory drought-insurance pilot with the Government of Lao PDR—the first time a Southeast Asian government has secured pre-arranged finance designed to pay out before drought hits farms. The Ministry of Finance receives payouts when the Combined Drought Index, monitored by the Department of Meteorology and Hydrology, crosses a threshold using observations and forecasts. KPL cites about 1.2 million people exposed each year and average losses of USD 672 million (around 3.5% of GDP), with El Niño risk for 2026–27. Payouts fund government-led early action: loudspeaker warnings, training of deputy village heads and volunteers by DMH and Lao National Radio, and drought-resistant cropping and irrigation support via the National Agriculture and Forestry Research Institute. Standard operating procedures were jointly developed by FAO with the Ministry of Finance, Ministry of Agriculture and Environment, Ministry of Labour and Social Welfare, and DMH. MAE’s Thevarack Phonekeo, Deputy Director-General of Planning and Cooperation, is quoted on earlier, more predictable support. The product extends Lao PDR’s 2025 SEADRIF multi-peril parametric sovereign policy, which paid USD 2 million in September 2025 after cyclones Wutip and Wipha. The pilot is framed as a sandbox for claims, payout and fund-flow systems, with a GCF Readiness feasibility study on scaling into social-protection channels.
signals.why_it_matters: Drought is the largest disaster risk for Lao rural cohorts who will farm and eat through the next El Niño. Pre-arranged sovereign payouts tied to an official drought index move climate finance from post-disaster begging to a Ministry of Finance instrument that can reach villages before harvests fail. The intergenerational mechanism is residual-risk transfer: today’s parametric trigger and SOP design decide whether later rural generations inherit a standing early-action purse or repeated uninsured losses at 3.5% of GDP.

signals.title: Madagascar Issues Interministerial Arrêté 4197-2026 Recognising Other Effective Area-Based Conservation Measures
signals.summary: On 5 March 2026 Madagascar issued interministerial Arrêté n°4197-2026 setting the process for recognising a site as an Other Effective Area-Based Conservation Measure (AMCE/OECM). The Ministry of Environment and Sustainable Development posted the instrument and its methodological annex during a 5–9 May 2026 coastal vulgarisation workshop in Fort-Dauphin (Anosy/Androy), held under the GEF6 marine-protected-area project. The annex states that recognition requires a dedicated AMCE working group (terms of reference already adopted by the Sydney CoPil overseeing the 2014 promise to triple marine protected area), Free, Prior and Informed Consent contextualised to Madagascar’s public-participation arrêté and Nagoya Protocol decree, and reporting of recognised sites to the World Database on OECMs. Two pilot sites (TGRN Ambakivao / Manambolo-Tsiribihina and the AQUALMA bird sanctuary in Mahajamba Bay) were already validated by the CoPil. The same MEDD page records that a new implementing decree of the 2015 protected-area code (COAP) was adopted by the Council of Government in July 2025; that decree is a 2025 event and is not filed separately. No MEDD HTML page for a completed CDN 3.0 deposit was retrieved; UNFCCC still lists Madagascar NDC 2 (January 2024).
signals.why_it_matters: Madagascar’s biodiversity and coastal commons are the living inheritance of later cohorts, but community-managed and privately conserved areas have lacked a legal path into the national conservation account. An interministerial arrêté that names OECM recognition, FPIC, and World Database reporting is the attempt to lock those sites into standing biodiversity governance rather than leaving them as informal local practice. Mechanism: Arrêté interministériel n°4197-2026 of 5 March 2026 on AMCE recognition, with a domesticated IUCN methodology annex requiring FPIC before evaluation.

signals.title: Mauritius Budget 2026-2027 Creates a Just Transition Commission and Allocates Rs 4 Billion to Coastal Climate Adaptation
signals.summary: On 19 June 2026 Prime Minister and Minister of Finance Navinchandra Ramgoolam presented Budget 2026-2027 to the National Assembly. Under Anchor 11 (Environment Enhancement) the speech earmarks Rs 4 billion for the Coastal Erosion Adaptation Programme, to rehabilitate more than 11.5 km of severely eroded shoreline across 17 priority sites over five years, with nature-based complements (reforestation, wetlands, dunes, coastal vegetation) and a National Shoreline Management Strategy. It revives the Maurice Ile Durable project and provides for a Just Transition Commission to lay foundations for an ecological and just society, including democratisation of the economy. The annex to the speech phases the Corporate Climate Responsibility levy onto the Advance Payment System (25% in FY 2026/27, rising to full APS in FY 2029/30) and disallows unused tax-credit offsets against the levy. The Public Sector Investment Programme 2026/27–2030/31 schedules Rs 23.16 billion through the Climate and Sustainability Fund over five years. Housing and youth measures in the same sitting (Rs 2 billion off-site infrastructure for 8,000 social-housing units; re-establishment of NICE under the PMO) are part of the same budget but are not treated as separate signals.
signals.why_it_matters: Coastal erosion and storm damage already shift reconstruction and land-loss costs onto later Mauritian cohorts. Putting a multi-year shoreline programme, a climate levy, and a Just Transition Commission into the annual appropriation is the attempt to make adaptation and transition costs a standing fiscal claim rather than residual disaster spending. Mechanism: Budget Speech 2026-2027 sitting of 19 June 2026 creating a Just Transition Commission and earmarking Rs 4 billion for coastal adaptation, with CCR levy APS phasing in the Finance Bill annex.

signals.title: Mauritius Climate Change Committee Approves Second Statutory Report Tracking NDC 3.0, CCR Levy and Climate Fund
signals.summary: On 1 July 2026 Mauritius’s Climate Change Committee, chaired by Permanent Secretary Jeanne Lan Hing Po, approved its Second Report under the Climate Change Act 2020. The official PDF records that Government agreed NDC 3.0 on 26 September 2025 and submitted it to the UNFCCC on 29 September 2025, with a 40% economy-wide GHG cut by 2035 versus BAU. It reports Corporate Climate Responsibility levy collections of Rs 7.623 billion to end-April 2026, Climate and Sustainability Fund spending of Rs 1.8436 billion from July 2025 to May 2026 (dominated by national flood/drainage works), and estimated climate-related public spending of Rs 7.9 billion (3.25% of appropriated expenditure), 77% adaptation. 2026 follow-through includes a 24–26 February SIDS NDC-implementation forum in Mauritius, UNEP Copenhagen Climate Centre assistance to strengthen NDC 3.0 (USD 231,771.64; national consultation launched 2026; data template circulated April 2026), and a World Bank NDC 3.0 Investment and Implementation Plan. The Ministry of Youth and Sports sits on the Committee. Corpus rg found no Mauritius NDC 3.0 / Climate Change Committee 2026 / CCR levy match.

A statutory committee report that names NDC 3.0, a corporate climate levy, and a joint public-private Climate and Sustainability Fund converts those choices into a standing accountability artefact rather than a one-off pledge. Mechanism: Climate Change Act 2020 committee report approved 1 July 2026, locking a 40% by-2035 NDC, CCR levy receipts, and earmarked adaptation/mitigation expenditure into the official monitoring cycle.

signals.title: Moldova Enacts Law 53/2026 Reforming Environment Institutions, Adding Mandatory GHG Monitoring to Permits and a Climate-Risk Hydromet Authority
signals.summary: On 9 April 2026 Parliament adopted Law No. 53 for amending certain normative acts (reform of authorities subordinate to the Ministry of Environment). President Maia Sandu promulgated it by Decree No. 586-X of 23 April 2026 (official PDF on presedinte.md). State news agency MOLDPRES the same day reports the statute reorganises the State Hydrometeorological Service into a public Authority for Meteorology and Environmental Monitoring to manage risks from climate change and extreme weather; requires environmental permits to include greenhouse-gas emissions monitoring; creates a 24-hour environmental-alert unit in the Environmental Protection Inspectorate; establishes a public institution for State Protected Natural Areas; and inserts into the Subsoil and Urbanism Codes an annual 0.25% contribution from the environmental-restoration financial guarantee. CIS legislation notes the same Law 53 as the 9 April 2026 amendment to Law 74/2024 on climate actions, in force from 25 April 2026. lex.justice.md / legis.md full article text was not retrieved in this scan; substance of climate-risk and GHG-permit clauses is taken from MOLDPRES plus the presidential promulgation of the numbered statute. Distinct from Moldova’s May 2025 NDC 3.0 and from 2024 Law 74 itself.
signals.why_it_matters: Moldova’s climate-neutrality-by-2050 law only binds later cohorts if hydromet, inspectorate and permit systems can actually measure GHG and extreme-weather risk. Mechanism: a promulgated 2026 organic-package statute (Law 53/2026, Decree 586-X) that rebuilds the climate-risk hydromet authority, writes GHG monitoring into environmental permits, and earmarks 0.25% of restoration guarantees for rehabilitation rather than leaving climate and pollution residuals on the next generation.

signals.title: Mozambique Agriculture Ministry Publishes NDC 3.0 Draft With Youth-Equity Theme and a 2026–2035 Mitigation Target
signals.summary: In February 2026 Mozambique’s Ministry of Agriculture, Environment and Fisheries posted a Portuguese NDC 3.0 draft (filename dated 28 January 2026) covering 2026–2035. The text records that a provisional NDC 3.0 was submitted to the UNFCCC on 5 November 2025 and presents this document as the second update. Cross-cutting theme 2 is “strengthening equity for women, youth and vulnerable communities,” citing Constitution articles 121–125 (children, women, youth, older persons, persons with disabilities) and stating the NDC should turn women and youth from victims/beneficiaries into drivers of climate action and just transition. The ICTU table sets a cumulative mitigation contribution of at least 3% versus BAU over 2026–2035, described as equivalent to 45% of the 2020 emissions level, on a revised 2020 baseline of 19,757 Gg CO2eq excluding LULUCF and 68,870 Gg including LULUCF. Several sections remain marked for a later version, including the NDC 2.0-to-3.0 change summary. UNFCCC NDCREG still lists only the 5 November 2025 provisional English PDF as active. No 2026 climate statute was retrieved from the Boletim da República.
signals.why_it_matters: Mozambique ranks among the world’s most disaster-exposed countries, so the 2026–2035 NDC is the residual emissions and adaptation path that later cohorts will inherit after cyclones, drought and displacement. Naming youth and women as a constitutional cross-cutting theme, while still leaving the mitigation number provisional, is the attempt to write intergenerational and gender equity into the Paris cycle before the final registry text. Mechanism: ministry-published NDC 3.0 draft (28 January 2026) with a quantified 2026–2035 mitigation ICTU table and an explicit youth-equity cross-cut, not yet replacing the November 2025 UNFCCC provisional.

signals.title: Oman Registers NDC 3.0 at UNFCCC With a 7–33% GHG Cut by 2035 Against a 2024 Baseline
signals.summary: On 30 July 2026 the UNFCCC NDC registry marked Oman’s NDC 3.0 active (English PDF posted the same day at 09:14). The Environment Authority submitted the third Nationally Determined Contribution as the national policy document for climate targets through 2035, aligned with Oman Vision 2040 and net-zero by 2050. ONA, reprinted by Oman Observer on 3 August 2026, states a 2024 baseline of about 93.6 million tonnes CO2-equivalent, an unconditional 7% cut by 2035, and a further 26% conditional on international finance, technology and capacity support, for a potential 33% total. Mitigation covers energy, industrial processes, agriculture and land use, and waste, with emphasis on renewables, efficiency, green hydrogen, circular economy and CCUS feasibility. Adaptation priorities include water, agriculture, fisheries, public health, tourism and infrastructure against drought, heat, cyclones, floods and sea-level rise. ONA records that the text was prepared with government, private-sector and specialised institutions. A direct GET of the UNFCCC PDF on 16 August 2026 returned a Cloudflare interstitial; the registry row and ONA figures are the fetched evidence.
signals.why_it_matters: Oman is a hydrocarbon exporter whose later cohorts inherit both residual emissions and climate-physical risk in water, coasts and heat. Registering NDC 3.0 locks a 2024 inventory and a 2026–2035 residual path so today’s energy mix, hydrogen bets and conditional-finance gap determine the climate space after 2035 and the 2050 net-zero claim. Mechanism: a Paris Agreement NDC 3.0 on the UNFCCC registry, prepared by the Environment Authority, with ONA’s explicit present-and-future-generations framing and no youth-governance seats quoted on the fetched ONA page.

signals.title: Panama Gazettes Executive Decree 4 Replacing the 20-Year EIA Regime with Climate Criteria
signals.summary: On 28 May 2026 Gaceta Oficial No. 30534-B listed Ministerio de Ambiente Executive Decree No. 4 regulating Chapter III of Title II of the consolidated text of Law 41 of 1998 on the environmental-impact-assessment process and issuing other provisions. MiAmbiente’s 29 May 2026 institutional notice states that the new executive decree replaces EIA rules in force for more than 20 years, after public consultation that the ministry says followed its internal FPIC procedures and Escazú guidelines. The notice says the instrument covers principles, criteria and procedures for preparing, filing, evaluating, approving, updating, modifying, monitoring and controlling EIA studies; adds digital platforms for environmental procedures; strengthens citizen participation and environmental-information access; and—material for this lane—includes climate-change adaptation and mitigation criteria in EIA studies. This is an implementing regulation of the General Environment Law, not the still-unenacted draft Ley Marco de Cambio Climático y Transición Verde (public consultation in May 2025; NDC 3.0 of 27 November 2025 remains the 2025 pledge).
signals.why_it_matters: Panama’s canal, coasts and forests lock land-use and infrastructure choices that later cohorts cannot cheaply unwind. Folding climate adaptation and mitigation into the EIA gate means new public and private works must account for residual climate risk before they are licensed, rather than leaving that risk as an after-the-fact disaster bill. Mechanism: Executive Decree 4 of 28 May 2026 replacing the long-standing EIA regulation under Law 41 of 1998, with climate criteria and Escazú-style participation, while the framework climate bill is still only a draft.

signals.title: Paraguay Submits NDC 3.0 With Economy-Wide 10% Net Cut and Child Climate Diagnosis to 2035
signals.summary: On 6 November 2025 Paraguay’s MADES formally submitted its Third Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC 3.0) and Second Adaptation Communication to the UNFCCC after Comisión Nacional de Cambio Climático validation. Resolución MADES N.º 281/2025 had opened a participatory build: kick-off 12 May 2025, 765 technical interactions with more than 70 institutions, public consultation 25 August–26 September 2025 reaching about 3,000 people, and more than 1,770 participants across the whole process. The UNFCCC technical annex (October 2025) sets child-specific adaptation targets 20–21: update by 2035 the national diagnostic on girls, boys and adolescents facing climate change, then implement at least 50% of its priority actions with the State, civil society and cooperation partners. Paraguay’s official Article 6.4 host-Party form states an unconditional 10% net GHG reduction by 2030 and 2035 on an economy-wide inventory basis. On 8 July 2026 MADES held the first Mesa Interinstitucional de Seguimiento de la NDC to protocol implementation of NDC 3.0 and the 2CA.
signals.why_it_matters: Paraguay is missing from the corpus. NDC 3.0 is the 2026–2035 Paris pledge that decides how much residual emissions, land conversion and climate risk today’s agribusiness and energy path leaves for children. Embedding a child-climate diagnostic and a 50% implementation target creates a measurable intergenerational accountability hook; the 10% unconditional net cut is the fiscal-and-land constraint that either funds that hook or displaces it.

signals.title: Poland Opens Official KPOZP Preconsultations on Draft National Restoration Plan Starting With Marine Chapter on 2 April 2026
signals.summary: On 2 April 2026 Poland's Climate and Environment Ministry held the first remote preconsultation meeting on the National Plan for Restoration of Natural Resources (Krajowy Plan Odbudowy Zasobów Przyrodniczych, KPOZP), covering the marine chapter (Article 5). The official page dated 3 April 2026 reports about 50 participants from fisheries, offshore renewables, NGOs, local government, national parks and nature authorities discussing proposed restoration measures and how to reconcile restoration with marine economic uses. The ministry NRL hub states Poland is preparing the KPOZP to show how, when and where Regulation (EU) 2024/1991 targets will be met, including 20% of EU land and sea by 2030 and all ecosystems in need of restoration by 2050. Full public consultation on a complete draft was still described as forthcoming on 16 August 2026; no Commission-format full-draft consultation page was located.

The assistance is meant to unify assessment systems, data collection, institutional coordination and a nationally prioritised plan to protect communities and critical infrastructure. Deadline 24 August 2026, 23:59 GMT+2 on Grant+; clarification closed 10 August 2026; information session was 15 July 2026; expected agreement start 26 October 2026. Non-members may apply if they file a Santiago Network membership EOI within the deadline.

Mechanism: a nationally endorsed L&D/GLOF plan is the pipeline that lets Nepal convert mountain climate harm into sequenced public investment and FRLD/climate-finance requests before the next outburst event locks in uncompensated losses.

signals.title: Slovenia Opens Public Consultation on Draft National Restoration Plan Through 9 August 2026 Ahead of 1 September Commission Submission
signals.summary: On 10 July 2026 Slovenia's Ministry of the Environment and Spatial Planning opened a public display of the draft National Restoration Plan (Nacionalni načrt za obnovo narave, NNON) through 9 August 2026, with comments to nnon.mop@gov.si. The official GOV.SI notice states the NNON is Slovenia's central instrument for Regulation (EU) 2024/1991, setting restoration measures for terrestrial, coastal, freshwater and marine ecosystems, urban ecosystems, pollinators, and agricultural and forest ecosystems, with EU-level targets of restoring at least 20% of land and sea by 2030 and all ecosystems in need of restoration by 2050. After the display, comments will be used to prepare a final draft for a Government decision and transmission to the Commission by 1 September 2026; a second public display and inter-ministerial alignment would follow Commission remarks. The ministry published the draft NNON PDF, an measures spreadsheet, a public-participation report and a socio-economic impact analysis. The process page records hundreds of earlier stakeholder responses and a 14 January 2026 Brdo workshop.
signals.why_it_matters: Slovenia is converting the EU restoration duty into a national 2030/2040/2050 timetable with a statutory-style public display immediately before the Commission deadline. Mechanism: a draft NRP with published measures and a socio-economic impact annex decides which degraded ecosystems are repaired this decade and how restoration costs and land-use constraints are shared across generations, so later cohorts do not inherit an unfunded restoration deficit.

signals.title: Sweden Agencies Deliver Draft National Restoration Plan to Government on 27 February 2026 With No Remiss Yet Announced
signals.summary: Boverket's official nature-restoration page states that the government-commissioned proposal for Sweden's National Restoration Plan, prepared with Naturvårdsverket, HaV, Skogsstyrelsen and Jordbruksverket, was submitted to the government on 27 February (2026 in the assignment context; the page discusses the September 2026 Commission filing). Boverket explicitly records that the government has not yet said whether it will circulate the plan for remiss (public consultation). signals.title: Venezuela Enacts Special Housing-Rental Law Naming Youth as Primary Beneficiaries
signals.summary: On 31 July 2026 the National Assembly sanctioned the Ley del Régimen Especial de Arrendamiento de Inmuebles Destinados a Vivienda (27 articles). Acting President Delcy Rodríguez promulgated it on 7 August 2026; Gaceta Oficial N.º 7.065 Extraordinario of that date brings it into force. Article 2 applies only to new contracts; existing tenancies stay under the 2011 rental-control law and the arbitrary-eviction decree. Article 3.1 states the primary purpose is to foster rental housing as a complementary, transitory route to the human right to housing, ‘especialmente dentro del sector de la juventud’. The official Assembly dispatch records free stipulation of the canon (with IPC adjustment if priced in bolívares), deposits or insurance up to three months returned in 15 days, a 30% monthly-canon threshold splitting major/minor repairs, a purchase-preference for solvent tenants after two years, mediation/arbitration, and municipal or arbitral eviction orders. The transitory provision exempts new contracts from the prior anti-eviction decree.
signals.why_it_matters: Venezuela is missing from the corpus. The statute reallocates housing opportunity toward new, especially young, tenants by creating a more flexible formal rental market while leaving the sitting (typically older) tenant cohort on the old protective regime. Who gains access to a first independent dwelling, and who bears eviction and deposit risk, is now split by contract date—an intergenerational housing-access rule, not a climate slogan.

signals.title: Vietnam Directive 31/CT-TTg Orders Universal Preschool 3–5 and Compulsory Lower-Secondary for 2026–27
signals.summary: On 5 August 2026 the Prime Minister issued Directive 31/CT-TTg on priority tasks for school year 2026–2027, published in full on the Government policy portal. Implementing Politburo Resolution 71-NQ/TW (22 August 2025) on an education-and-training breakthrough, the directive orders the Ministry of Education and Training and provincial chairs to shift from ‘education administration’ to ‘education-development governance’. Core equity measures include rolling out universal preschool for children aged 3–5 and compulsory lower-secondary education; piloting a new early-childhood curriculum; supplying a single national textbook set before 15 August 2026; consolidating substandard satellite schools in remote, border and ethnic-minority areas into boarding/semi-boarding schools at main sites; and prioritising resources so pupils in ethnic-minority, mountain, border, island and especially disadvantaged localities get equal access to quality education, narrowing regional and school-level gaps. It also requires completing teacher recruitment for 2026–27, attraction policies for hard-to-staff subjects and difficult areas, two-session days, STEM/STEAM and digital skills, and public VET network restructuring with post-lower-secondary vocational streaming.
signals.why_it_matters: Who completes preschool and lower secondary in 2026–27 decides the skill and health baseline of the next working-age cohort, especially in mountain and Mekong-Delta ethnic-minority districts. The directive is the annual implementation instrument for Resolution 71-NQ/TW: a Prime Ministerial order that makes universal 3–5 preschool, compulsory lower secondary, and gap-closing boarding provision duties of MOET and every province for this school year, not a distant plan.

signals.title: Vietnam Issues Resolution 208/NQ-CP Operationalising Party Climate Conclusion 75-KL/TW for 2026–2030
signals.summary: On 4 August 2026 Vietnam’s Government issued Resolution 208/NQ-CP, signed by Deputy Prime Minister Hồ Quốc Dũng, promulgating the Government Action Programme to implement Party Central Committee Conclusion 75-KL/TW of 28 July 2026 on environmental protection and proactive climate-change response in the new period. The official Government Portal notice of 5 August states that ministries and provincial People’s Committees must build plans for 2026–2030 (vision to 2045) with a single lead agency, deadline, product and resource envelope for each task. Nine solution groups cover public education; law and enforcement; resource mobilisation; pollution control; biodiversity; climate adaptation and disaster-risk reduction; green, circular and low-carbon transition plus GHG management; science, digitalisation and human resources; and international cooperation. Adaptation measures include climate-resilient construction standards, storm/flood/drought/salinity-resistant infrastructure, climate-resilient cities, climate-smart agriculture, and region-specific nature- and community-based adaptation for the northern midlands, central coast and Mekong Delta, including relocating settlements from high-risk zones while protecting livelihoods and health care. Gazette metadata on congbao.chinhphu.vn records issuance and effect on 4 August 2026 (Công báo 471).
signals.why_it_matters: Vietnam’s Mekong Delta and coastal cities already shift flood, salinity and livelihood risk onto later cohorts. A Government resolution that turns a Central Committee climate conclusion into a 2026–2030 task matrix with named leads and resources is the mechanism that decides whether net-zero-2050 and green-economy targets become budgeted public duties rather than Party language. The intergenerational channel is residual-risk assignment: today’s siting, wastewater, circular-economy and Mekong-Delta relocation choices determine the climate and health space inherited after 2030.

signals.title: Vietnam Replaces 2021 Youth Strategy With Decision 1184/QĐ-TTg Adding Green Jobs and Climate Skills
signals.summary: On 1 July 2026 Deputy Prime Minister Phạm Thị Thanh Trà signed Prime Ministerial Decision 1184/QĐ-TTg approving an adjusted Vietnam Youth Development Strategy 2021–2030, effective the same day and replacing Decision 1331/QĐ-TTg of 24 July 2021. The Official Gazette records issuer Thủ tướng Chính phủ, Công báo 395. The decision, grounded in the 2020 Youth Law and Government Resolution 349/NQ-CP of 27 October 2025, instructs every ministry and provincial People’s Committee to fold youth targets into five-year and annual socio-economic plans, with the Ministry of Home Affairs as standing lead and provincial People’s Councils to amend local youth resolutions. Quantified 2030 targets include youth unemployment/underemployment below 6%; 40% of youth participating in green or circular-economy activities; 70% of youth in decent, green, digital or high-tech jobs; annual training of 70% of youth in disaster, climate-change, epidemic and environmental response; 15% of youth in state/political-social organisations holding leadership posts (at least 30% of those women); 20% of youth in those organisations placed in leadership pipelines; and legal/sandbox access for youth to digital, green and circular business models. State budget is the core financing source, with international aid and social mobilisation as supplements. Implementation is to be reviewed annually and summed in Q4 2030.
signals.why_it_matters: Vietnam’s existing corpus youth signals are a 2025 NDC-roadmap launch and a 2024 civil-society summit demand. Decision 1184 is the statutory replacement of the 2021 youth strategy, converting those demands into quantified green-job, climate-skill and leadership-quota duties that provinces must budget through 2030. The intergenerational mechanism is a Prime Ministerial strategy with named fiscal and personnel leads: later cohorts inherit either a tracked pipeline into green work and public office or another decade of unfunded youth rhetoric.

signals.title: West Virginia Enacts Youth Summer Employment and Career Readiness Act for Ages 14–20
signals.summary: Committee Substitute for House Bill 5480, the West Virginia Youth Summer Employment and Career Readiness Act, passed the Legislature on 14 March 2026, became law without the Governor’s signature on 2 April 2026, took effect 90 days after passage on 12 June 2026, and was chaptered as Chapter 142, Acts, Regular Session, 2026 on 29 June 2026. New article §5B-2P creates a statewide paid summer employment programme in the Department of Commerce’s Division of Workforce Development for youth aged 14–20, with grant-funded placements at private, nonprofit and public employer partners. Legislative findings name youth out-migration and workforce shortages; programme design must emphasise high-demand sectors, public service, entrepreneurship and regional career pathways, coordinated with the Department of Education and county boards. Participants must be paid at least the state minimum wage; employers may not displace existing staff. A special revenue “West Virginia Youth Summer Employment and Career Readiness Fund” is created; for FY ending 30 June 2026 and 2027, expenditures from collections are authorised without a separate appropriation. The department’s first report to the Governor and Joint Committee is due 1 December 2026.
signals.why_it_matters: West Virginia’s youth leave because the first paid job is elsewhere. A statutory summer-wage programme for 14–20-year-olds is an attempt to keep this cohort attached to in-state work before out-migration hardens, so the next generation inherits a local labour market rather than an emptied one. The special fund and 2026–27 collection-spending authority put current public money on that first rung instead of treating youth joblessness as a later welfare cost.

signals.title: Zambia Assents to Food Reserve Act 6/2026, Rebuilding the National Strategic Food Reserve
signals.summary: The Food Reserve Act, 2026 (Act No. 6 of 2026) was assented on 31 March 2026 and published in the Government Gazette supplement on 8 April 2026. It repeals and replaces the Food Reserve Act, 2020, continues the Food Reserve Agency as a body corporate, reconstitutes its Board, and continues the National Strategic Food Reserve. Section 16 states the reserve’s purposes: ensuring availability of designated commodities for national food security; meeting domestic shortfalls; mitigating hardship of vulnerable households under the Disaster Management Act; meeting emergency food shortages; and, with Cabinet approval, foreign food aid. The Minister must designate essential commodities by statutory instrument at least 60 days before 31 October each year; the Agency must publish a purchase plan in the Gazette at least 30 days before 10 May, prioritising rural markets, and may sell for stock rotation, emergency relief, local shortfalls or community sales to essential-service institutions and vulnerable groups. Commencement is by ministerial statutory instrument; ZambiaLII records the Act as uncommenced as of the 8 April 2026 version. Distinct from already-ingested Zambia Acts 12/2026 (youth PR seats) and 34/2026 (NYDC amendment).
signals.why_it_matters: A statutory grain reserve is how a drought-exposed country allocates this year’s harvest between present consumers and the children who will need food in the next shock. By forcing annual designation, Gazette purchase plans and rural-priority buying, the Act tries to stop today’s market from emptying the cupboard that later cohorts rely on when prices spike or rains fail. Until the Minister commences it, that intergenerational buffer remains on paper.

signals.title: ACERWC Continental Study Recommends Child-Rights Impact Assessments for African Climate Policies and Projects
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: On 7–8 April 2025 the African Committee of Experts on the Rights and Welfare of the Child (ACERWC), an African Union organ, published and launched its Continental Study on Climate Change and Children’s Rights in Africa during the 45th Ordinary Session. The study treats intergenerational equity as a core concept and, applying Article 4(1) of the African Children’s Charter (the child’s best interests as ‘the primary consideration’), states that policies and projects that may affect children in the climate context should be accompanied by a child-rights impact assessment examining effects and recommending alternatives. It also urges subjecting climate-finance execution and loss-and-damage mechanisms to CRIA, and integrating child-rights, human-rights and environmental impact assessments rather than running parallel processes. The recommendation is interpretive and recommendatory, not a binding AU regulation or a national statute.
signals.why_it_matters: This is the closest continental IIA-cousin methodology yet issued by an AU organ: it tells African Charter states who must assess what (state authorities, before climate policies, NAPs, projects and climate-finance execution), against which legal test (Article 4(1) best interests as the primary consideration, plus intergenerational equity), and with what force (Charter interpretation by the treaty body, not a self-executing CRIA regulation). It fills the Agenda 2063 gap — 2063 has no child-rights IA tool — and is distinct from the already-ingested January 2026 ACERWC African Court observations and the April 2026 47th-session decision to draft NDC/NAP child-rights guidelines.

signals.title: Austria's Binding Jugend-Check Requires Child and Youth Impact Assessment of All Federal Bills
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: Since 1 January 2013 Austria's Jugend-Check has been a mandatory dimension of the federal Wirkungsorientierte Folgenabschätzung (WFA). The Federal Chancellery states that a regulation obliges every ministry to assess draft laws' effects on children and young people before adoption, as part of the two-stage WFA published with the consultation draft and government bill. Legal bases are Art. 51(8) B-VG and §§ 17–18 Bundeshaushaltsgesetz 2013, implemented by the WFA-Kinder-und-Jugend-Verordnung (BGBl. II Nr. 495/2012), still in force in the RIS consolidation of 1 August 2026. Simplified screening asks whether protection, care, child-cost compensation or medium-term Zukunftssicherung of children and young adults is affected; material cases require a deeper assessment. The 2025 Youth Strategy implementation report (Ministerrat 9 July 2025) keeps Reality Checks alongside the WFA duty but does not replace it.
signals.why_it_matters: This is a binding CRWIA-style IIA cousin: ministries must complete a child-and-youth impact assessment before a federal law or major financially significant project is adopted, and the result travels with the bill. Unlike Germany's administrative Jugend-Check, Austria's duty sits in budget law and a still-current special ordinance, including a forward-looking 'future security' test. The instrument is missing from the GYC corpus despite being one of the oldest statutory youth-impact gates in Europe.

signals.title: Balearic Law 7/2024 Repeals Mandatory Budget and Annual Wellbeing Impact Assessments from Ley 10/2023
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: Ley 7/2024 of 11 December (BOE 17 January 2025, BOE-A-2025-720) converts Decreto-ley 3/2024 and permanently guts Spain's first future-generations statute. The derogatory provision expressly repeals Articles 7 and 8 of Ley 10/2023: the duty to make visible in budget-programme memoranda how spending advances wellbeing objectives for future generations, and the duty of public bodies to send large works contracts, subsidy plans and strategic projects to the Comisión for an annual impact report to Parliament. Article 6 is rewritten so the former mandatory wellbeing impact report on bills, regulations, territorial plans and sectoral plans — with a public Commission opinion and a duty to consider alternatives after an unfavourable opinion — is replaced by optional civil-society comments in prior consultation. Commission functions shrink to voluntary guidance, on-request advice 'if workload allows', and reports on matters outside Balearic competence. The delayed-entry clause that had kept Titles II–III inoperative until the Commission was constituted and guides approved is deleted, so the hollowed-out statute is immediately in force. Corpus rg found the 2023 enactment (baleares-ley-10-2023) but no 2024/2025 rollback.
signals.why_it_matters: This is a documented IIA rollback: the Balearic Government and Parliament stripped the only Iberian statute that required a wellbeing/future-generations impact assessment before budgets and norms were adopted. Mechanism lost: promoter-prepared impact reports plus Commission opinion inside the legislative and budget dossier, replaced by a non-binding orientation duty and optional consultation comments. The Commission remains on paper as a consultative body with no budget-IIA or annual evaluation mandate. For the 'does it bite?' test, Ley 10/2023 never had to prove it could change a budget because the teeth were removed before the delayed-entry conditions were met.

signals.title: Canada’s Amended Impact Assessment Act Still Requires a Sustainability Test for Present and Future Generations
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: Canada’s Impact Assessment Act (IAA) remains the closest federal Americas cousin to an intergenerational impact assessment, and it is missing from the GYC corpus. Section 2 defines sustainability as the ability to protect the environment, contribute to social and economic well-being, and preserve health ‘in a manner that benefits present and future generations.’ Section 22(1)(h) requires every impact assessment of a designated project to take into account the extent to which the project contributes to sustainability. Section 63(c), as amended in 2024, then forces the Minister or Governor in Council, before finding significant adverse federal effects justified in the public interest, to consider ‘the extent to which the effects that are likely to be caused by the carrying out of that project contribute to sustainability.’ The Impact Assessment Agency of Canada announced on 21 June 2024 that Budget Implementation Act, 2024, No. 1 received Royal Assent on 20 June 2024 and brought the amended IAA into force after the Supreme Court of Canada’s 2023 reference. The 2024 rewrite narrowed federal effects and the public-interest test but kept the statutory sustainability/future-generations definition and the s. 63(c) decision factor. The Justice Laws consolidation fetched on 17 August 2026 is current to a 6 August 2026 page update. This is a project-level environmental impact gate, not a general IIA for bills or budgets.
signals.why_it_matters: Mechanism: the Impact Assessment Agency must assess, and the Minister or Governor in Council must weigh, whether a designated project’s effects contribute to sustainability defined as benefits for present and future generations, before a public-interest approval and before legally binding conditions issue under s. 64. Who: federal decision-makers on designated projects (not every law or budget). Legal force: statute; proponents must comply with decision-statement conditions. It is the strongest enacted Americas EIA-IE test found in this lane, but it is not a Wales/Italy-style IIA that screens ordinary legislation.

signals.title: CEPAL Issues a December 2025 Anticipatory-Governance Guide with Dynamic Evaluation, Not a Statutory IIA Method
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: On 8 December 2025 CEPAL published Guía básica de gobernanza anticipatoria (LC/MEX/TS.2025/17, 80 pages, Vargas Lama / Rosado / Oddone, Mexico subregional office). A 12 December 2025 CEPAL briefing note presents it as a practical tool for Latin American and Caribbean public officials to exit short-term reactive management. Chapter IV covers multitemporal measurement, dynamic evaluation and strategic adjustment. Recommendations include institutionalising a long-term vision, creating transversal anticipation units, establishing multitemporal legal frameworks, stable resources, public-leadership training, learning networks, state political pacts, standing citizen participation, and making monitoring a learning process. The guide is linked to the Red de Comisiones de Futuro Parlamentarias. Fetched text emphasises scenarios, multitemporal roadmaps and adaptive monitoring and evaluation. It does not define a statutory Intergenerational Impact Assessment, name who must run an IIA before a law or budget, or attach legal force. It is a later distinct CEPAL product from the June 2025 Second Regional Conference already in the corpus.

Legal force: none. It shows the regional UN body is building evaluation capacity around parliamentary futures commissions rather than exporting a Wales/Italy-style IIA statute — and no first Latin American statutory IIA was found alongside it.

signals.title: Council of Europe Youth Ministers Adopt Reference Framework Requiring Ex-Ante and Ex-Post Human-Rights Impact Assessments
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: On 8–9 October 2025 in Valletta, Council of Europe youth ministers adopted a Resolution annexing the Reference Framework on a Youth Perspective, distinct from the same-day Final Declaration already in the corpus. The Framework is a three-phase method (preparation; design and implementation; monitoring and evaluation) for integrating youth views across the policy cycle. In the design phase it tells authorities to 'consider conducting' human rights-based expert impact assessments of how policies affect young people before decisions (ex-ante) and after implementation (ex-post). Guiding principles explicitly include intergenerational justice and solidarity: today's decisions must be assessed for consequences on current and future generations. Ministers invited the Joint Council on Youth to develop practical tools (guidelines, checklists, training modules). The instrument is a ministerial standard for 46 member States, not a treaty with automatic legal minimums.
signals.why_it_matters: This is the first Council of Europe ministerial standard that writes youth/generational impact assessment into a shared operating method. Mechanism: member-State and CoE policymakers are asked, before adopting policies that concern young people, to run human rights-based ex-ante assessments and later ex-post evaluations involving youth organisations, with intergenerational justice as a named principle. Legal force is soft (consider/undertake) but it is the multilateral checklist that HUDERIA is not: HUDERIA is AI-specific, this Framework is general policymaking.

signals.title: Dutch Senate Instructs Government to Apply the Kinderrechtentoets to All Future Youth-Care Bills
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: On 7 October 2025 the Dutch Senate adopted motion 36.546, I (Perin-Gopie / Volt and others) asking the government to apply the Kinderrechtentoets as standard on all future youth-care bills, to record the outcomes in the explanatory memorandum, and to inform the Senate on implementation before the Christmas recess. PVV, FVD, JA21 and BBB voted against. The four-step Child Rights Impact Assessment was launched by the Kinderombudsman on 10 December 2024, with then State Secretary for Legal Protection Teun Struycken present, after the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child's 2022 recommendation that the Netherlands develop a CRIA. It is a screening-plus-full-assessment tool for laws and policies that affect children directly or indirectly. A broader motion to create a standing CRIA facility was rejected the same day. The VWS committee treated the adopted motion as partly executed on 26 May 2026 after written exchanges with the Minister for Long-term Care, Youth and Sport; a further motion to apply the test more widely was rejected on 7 April 2026. Implementation deadline recorded by the Senate is 1 July 2026.
signals.why_it_matters: The IIA mechanism is a parliamentary instruction that youth-care legislation must run a child-rights impact test before adoption and publish the result in the memorie van toelichting — converting an ombudsman toolkit into a sectoral pre-legislative duty. Legal force is a Senate motion, not a general statute: it covers future jeugdzorg bills rather than all law or the budget, and a later attempt to widen the duty failed. Distinct from the Netherlands' Generatietoets inside Beleidskompas already in the corpus.

signals.title: European Commission Documents Operational Youth Check as Mandatory Annex I Screen and Applies It to the 2026 Work Programme
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: The Commission's official Youth Check page sets out the operating method: it is mandatory for all Annex I initiatives in the Commission Work Programme; departments assess youth relevance, run youth consultations, and in some cases deepen the analysis in an impact-assessment report reviewed by the Regulatory Scrutiny Board. DG EAC advises, the Commission Youth Network and EU Youth Stakeholders Group support consultations, and the EU Youth Coordinator oversees the process. A progress note last updated 2 June 2026 lists 12 2025 Work Programme initiatives that were screened and consulted (including the post-2027 MFF, Quality Jobs Roadmap, Union of Skills and European Democracy Shield) and states the check is already being applied to 2026 Work Programme files. The 2026 consultation list on the method page includes the adopted Intergenerational Fairness Strategy, Circular Economy Act, Child Guarantee strengthening and climate-energy packages. This is process documentation, not a published Intergenerational Fairness Index methodology or a live Futures Balance AI tool; those remain 'Coming soon' / 'Development ongoing' on the strategy portal.
signals.why_it_matters: This is the post-March 2026 operationalisation of the youth-check limb of EU IIA. Mechanism: before the College adopts a key Work Programme initiative, the lead DG must assess youth relevance and consult young people; where an IA is required, youth impacts can go to the Regulatory Scrutiny Board. Legal force is internal Commission procedure (mandatory for Annex I), not a regulation imposing IIA on Member States. No separate youth-check handbook PDF was found; this portal page plus the June 2026 progress note are the official method.

signals.title: Flanders Expands Mandatory JoKER Child-and-Youth Impact Reports from Under-25 to Age 30
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: On 13 March 2026 the Flemish Government, after Council of State advice, finally approved a draft decree amending the Youth Decree of 23 November 2023 and submitted it to the Flemish Parliament (document 754 (2025-2026) No. 1, 19 March 2026). Article 2 replaces the JoKER trigger in Article 7 — a child-and-youth impact report that must accompany every government draft decree that directly affects young people — so the duty covers persons 'up to and including 30' rather than 'younger than 25', aligning JoKER with the decree's definition of youth. JoKER itself has been statutory since 1997 (KER) and 2008 (JoKER): ministers must describe effects on children and young people with and without the proposal, plus alternatives to avoid, limit or remedy serious harm, and the report is inserted in the explanatory memorandum's impact-analysis section. The Department of Culture, Youth and Media's official JoKER page now states the duty as applying to persons through age 30. JoKER remains required only for government draft decrees, not parliamentary members' bills, government decisions, ministerial orders or circulars.
signals.why_it_matters: JoKER is a binding regional IIA cousin: before a Flemish Government draft decree is laid in Parliament, the sponsoring minister must assess effects on children and young people and publish that assessment in the explanatory memorandum. Extending the cohort from under-25 to through age 30 brings late-youth housing, work and education impacts inside a statutory pre-legislative gate rather than leaving 26–30-year-olds outside the child-impact tool. Legal force is decree-level and limited to government bills; the Youth minister and Council of State police missing reports, but JoKER does not bind budgets or administrative decisions.

signals.title: France's 2016 Youth-Impact Clause Requires Intergenerational-Justice Analysis in Every Government Bill Study
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: The Prime Minister's circular of 2 May 2016 makes a 'clause d'impact jeunesse' mandatory in the ex-ante evaluation of government bills and regulatory texts. The official SGG mémento, still hosted on the government's administrative-documentation site, instructs ministries to analyse each draft against equality among young people, intergenerational justice and non-discrimination, 'necessarily' including a prospective dimension because measures affect both today's youth and tomorrow's. For bills this sits on top of the organic-law impact-study duty (loi organique 2009-403); for regulations a dedicated youth chapter or youth-specific impact sheet applies, focused on ages 16–25 (with 25–30 flagged where age barriers or housing/employment effects are large). Compensating measures are expected if a text would penalise current or future young cohorts. No 2025–26 statute upgrades the circular into a Wales/Italy-style IIA; the Cour des comptes 2025 youth-policy report reviews outcomes, not this clause.
signals.why_it_matters: The IIA mechanism is an administrative youth-and-future-youth test: every ministry must, before a government bill or regulation is adopted, document effects on 16–25-year-olds and on the next youth cohort, explicitly under the heading of intergenerational justice. Legal force is a Prime Minister circular plus the organic-law impact-study envelope—not a standalone IIA statute—so quality is uneven, but the instrument is the French national cousin and is missing from the corpus.

signals.title: Germany Youth-Check Third Report: 490 Federal Bills Screened, 91 Youth Impact Assessments in 20th Bundestag
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: On 23 September 2025 Federal Youth Minister Karin Prien received the Competence Centre Youth-Check (KomJC) Third Report on youth-specific regulatory impact assessment in the 20th Bundestag (2021–2025). KomJC, a project of the German Research Institute for Public Administration funded long-term by the federal youth ministry since 2023, screened 490 federal draft laws for effects on people aged 12–27 and published 91 full Jugend-Checks across six life domains (education/work, digital, family, leisure, politics/society, environment/health). Prien called youth-specific impact assessment 'not a luxury but a necessity' and a tool for intergenerational justice. The instrument remains administrative rather than statutory: it accompanies government bills but does not bind the Bundestag to amend them. Thuringia is piloting the first Land-level Jugend-Check through end-2026.
signals.why_it_matters: The IIA cousin is a standing youth regulatory impact assessment: an independent scientific unit must examine every federal government bill for intended and unintended effects on 12–27-year-olds before cabinet/parliamentary debate, then publish the check. Legal force is soft—sensitisation, not a veto—but the 2025 report is the first full-term evidence that the mechanism can run at scale (490 screens / 91 published checks) without delaying legislation. That is the missing German counterpart to Italy's VIG and the EU Youth Check, and it is absent from the GYC corpus (the existing Germany signal covers only the Bundestag sustainability council).
