signals.title: Ghana Enacts Environmental Protection Act 1124 Making Intergenerational Equity a Guiding Principle for EIA Enforcement
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: On 6 January 2025 the President of Ghana assented to the Environmental Protection Act, 2025 (Act 1124), gazetted as the 1,124th Act of Parliament. The statute repeals the Environmental Protection Agency Act, 1994 (Act 490), reconstitutes the regulator as the Environmental Protection Authority, and consolidates pesticides, hazardous-waste, e-waste and climate-response functions. Section 3(2)(b)(iii) requires the Authority to ensure compliance with laid-down environmental assessment procedures in the planning and implementation of policies, plans, programmes and projects. Section 29 lets the Authority require an environmental assessment of an undertaking, issue or renew an environmental permit, and block other organs of state from granting environment-affecting licences until the Authority has given written confirmation of EA compliance. Part Six section 161 then directs that, to ensure compliance with the Act, the Authority and other concerned persons shall be guided by five principles, including intergenerational equity. Section 170 defines intergenerational equity as meeting the needs of the present generation without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their needs, and defines an undertaking as a policy, plan, programme or project. The Authority later hosted companion Environmental Protection (Environmental Assessment) Regulations, 2025 (L.I. 2504) on its laws page as the replacement for L.I. 1652.
signals.why_it_matters: This is a 2025 African parent statute for environmental assessment that newly names intergenerational equity as a mandatory enforcement guide, not merely a constitutional slogan. Mechanism: before an environmental permit issues under section 29, and before other licensing bodies may approve an environment-affecting activity, the Environmental Protection Authority and concerned persons must apply the section 161(b) intergenerational-equity principle as defined in section 170, covering policies, plans, programmes and projects. Legal force is binding statute in force from 6 January 2025; the 2025 assessment regulations (L.I. 2504) are the procedural vehicle, but the IE test sits in the Act itself.

signals.title: Hungary's Ombudsman Act Requires a Formal Opinion on Draft Laws and Plans Directly Affecting Future Generations
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: Act CXI of 2011 on the Commissioner for Fundamental Rights, published in official English translation by the Commissioner's office, creates a standing statutory impact-review duty distinct from Hungary's 2025 climate-act annulment. Section 2(2) provides that the Commissioner shall give an opinion on draft legislation affecting his or her tasks and competences, on long-term development and spatial planning plans and concepts, and on plans and concepts otherwise directly affecting the quality of life of future generations, and may propose amendment or drafting of fundamental-rights legislation. Section 1(2)(b) requires special attention, including ex officio proceedings, to the interests of future generations as defined in Article P of the Fundamental Law. Section 3(1) assigns the Deputy Commissioner responsible for future generations (who may use the title Ombudsman for Future Generations) to monitor those interests, warn of rights infringements affecting future generations, propose ex officio inquiries and Constitutional Court referrals, monitor Parliament's sustainable development strategy, and propose legislation on the rights of future generations. This is an ombudsman opinion-and-challenge power over others' drafts, not a ministry-authored generational impact assessment that must accompany every government bill.
signals.why_it_matters: Hungary's IIA-equivalent is a binding review gate inside the NHRI, not an AIR-style VIG. Mechanism: before draft laws, long-term development plans, spatial plans, or other concepts that directly affect future generations' quality of life proceed, the Commissioner must be able to issue a statutory opinion; the Future Generations Deputy can escalate to investigation or Constitutional Court review. Legal force: Act CXI of 2011, still in force, with the Deputy using the Ombudsman for Future Generations title. This instrument was missing from the corpus as an impact-review statute; the existing operational-ombudsman signal covers continued activity and the climate ruling, not the Section 2(2) opinion duty on drafts and plans.

signals.title: Ireland Department of Finance Publishes Future Forty, a First 40-Year Fiscal Outlook to 2065
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: On 4 November 2025 Finance Minister Paschal Donohoe published Future Forty: A Fiscal and Economic Outlook to 2065, the Department of Finance's first Australia-IGR-style 40-year no-policy-change assessment of Ireland's public finances. The Strategic Economic Development Unit modelled a Central Scenario plus 2,187 alternatives covering demographics, climate, housing, healthcare, digitalisation, deglobalisation and EU enlargement. In the Central Scenario, age-related spending, slowing productivity and falling corporation-tax receipts drive the annual deficit toward 7.9% of GNI* and national debt to 148% of GNI* by 2065, with a narrowing window to 2037 in which the deficit stays below 3% of GNI*. The full report states that acting now on spending prioritisation would 'prevent an unsustainable debt burden on future generations' and cites Australia's 2023 Intergenerational Report as a comparator.
signals.why_it_matters: This is a finance-ministry Intergenerational Report used as a fiscal IIA: officials must now put a 40-year, no-policy-change picture of who will pay for ageing, climate and tax-base erosion in front of Budget and National Economic Dialogue decisions, even though the product is analytical rather than a statutory gate. Mechanism: Department of Finance Strategic Economic Development Unit publishes a recurring long-horizon fiscal test so today's expenditure choices can be judged against the debt left to later cohorts. It is Ireland's first official IGR analogue and is missing from the corpus.

signals.title: Ireland Runs a Cross-Government Workshop on a Child Rights and Youth Impact Assessment Toolkit
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: On 7 February 2025 Ireland’s then Department of Children, Equality, Disability, Integration and Youth hosted a Child Rights and Youth Impact Assessment (CRYIA) workshop for policymakers from several departments. Officials worked through a draft CRYIA tool on hypothetical policy scenarios. The department presents CRIA as a UNCRC general measure of implementation and a Young Ireland (2023–2028) commitment to develop a prototype and roll CRIA out across government and agencies by 2028. A 2024 EU CERV project with the Children’s Rights Alliance, University of Galway, Foróige, Tusla and Eurochild produced the draft instrument; DCEDIY’s 2024 annual report said the tool would be progressed and piloted in 2025. The Ombudsman for Children’s April 2026 UPR submission welcomes the toolkit but says further detail is still needed on government-wide rollout and uptake. No 2026 budget or flagship bill has a published mandatory CRYIA.
signals.why_it_matters: The IIA mechanism in design is a Child Rights and Youth Impact Assessment that departments would use to identify, research, analyse and record predicted effects of proposed decisions on children’s rights before policy or legislation is adopted. Legal force today is a national-framework commitment, not a statute: Young Ireland sets rollout by 2028, and the February 2025 workshop is capacity-building rather than a binding pre-legislative gate. If rolled out, Ireland would join Wales/Scotland-style CRIA practice without UNCRC incorporation.

signals.title: Justice Canada Publishes a Federal Child Rights Impact Assessment Tool, Still Voluntary for Cabinet
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: On 11 July 2023 Justice Canada launched a Child Rights Impact Assessment (CRIA) tool and 2.5-hour e-learning course, still live on the departmental site (page dated 25 July 2023; tool page fetched 17 August 2026). The tool is designed primarily for federal officials developing a law, policy, program or other initiative. It is grounded in the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, complements Gender-Based Analysis Plus, and uses a two-stage process: an early screening, then a full CRIA if any direct, indirect, intended or unintended child-rights effects are identified, including mitigation and, where possible, children’s views. Open Government tracker commitment C04.3.4 records the 11 July 2023 launch as complete. The official pages do not make CRIA mandatory for Memoranda to Cabinet. Bill S-212 (National Strategy for Children and Youth Act), which passed the Senate on 10 March 2026 and received first reading in the House on 12 March 2026, requires a national strategy with indicators and parliamentary reporting but does not create a CRIA duty. New Brunswick’s 2013 Cabinet CRIA, often cited as North America’s first mandatory CRIA, could not be confirmed on a current official gnb.ca page in 2025–26.
signals.why_it_matters: Mechanism: federal officials are given an official CRC-based template to assess child impacts of a proposed initiative before it is adopted, with a screening gate and a full assessment plus mitigation if effects are found. Who: Justice Canada and other federal departments (also usable by provinces and NGOs). Legal force: administrative guidance only — not a Cabinet or statutory mandate — so it is a cousin CRWIA, not an enacted IIA. It is the missing federal Canadian child-IA instrument; the 2025–26 S-212 strategy bill does not close that gap.

signals.title: Mexican Senators Table a Constitutional Duty to Evaluate Long-Term Fiscal Impacts of Public Debt
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: On 7 May 2025, PRI senators led by Alejandro Moreno Cárdenas filed with the Permanent Commission an initiative to reform Constitution Article 25 and add Article 134 Bis on equidad fiscal intergeneracional. The official SIL PDF (asun_4904191, 11 June 2025) would require the State to consider fiscal equity between present and future generations in national development, and would bind every federal, state and municipal public-debt contract to financial sustainability, transparency and intergenerational responsibility. Proposed 134 Bis would oblige the State to evaluate, justify and limit indebtedness: debt preferably for long-term public investment; no current-expenditure borrowing except national emergency; secondary laws to create ‘mecanismos de evaluación técnica y participación ciudadana para valorar los impactos fiscales a largo plazo’; a federal Fondo de Amortización Intergeneracional; and a national debt register for the states. Transitories give Congress 180 days for secondary legislation and the Executive 12 months to propose the fund. This is distinct from the 30 June 2025 García Medina bills for a Senate Comisión de Futuro already in the corpus. No DOF publication or enacted text was found. A separate November 2025 SIL fisheries initiative would add an intergenerational-equity principle to the General Fisheries Law without creating an IA procedure; a February 2026 commission dictamen was not confirmed on an official Diputados page.
signals.why_it_matters: This is the only verified 2025–26 Mexican national proposal that would force an impact-style test before a fiscal decision. Mechanism: if enacted, authorities could not contract public debt without evaluating and justifying long-term fiscal impacts under secondary technical-evaluation rules, with constitutional rank. Who: Federation, states and municipalities, before debt is taken on. Legal force: currently a Senate/Permanent Commission initiative only — proposed, not enacted — so Mexico still has no statutory IIA.

signals.title: New Zealand Repeals Statutory Wellbeing Report and Budget Wellbeing-Objective Duties
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: The Public Finance Amendment Act 2026 (2026 No 9) received Royal assent on 2 April 2026 after third reading on 31 March and came into force on 1 July 2026. Sections 17 and 21 repeal Public Finance Act 1989 s 26KB (wellbeing objectives that had to guide Budget decision-making and be explained in the Fiscal Strategy Report) and s 26NB (Treasury's at-least-four-yearly wellbeing report, first published as Te Tai Waiora in 2022). The consolidated Public Finance Act now marks both sections '[Repealed]' as of 1 July 2026. Finance Minister Nicola Willis's Beehive release on passage said the Act 'removes the need for Treasury to report on wellbeing' so it can focus on core economic and fiscal advice. Treasury's stewardship page was updated 16 June 2026 to record the repeal.

After the repeal, neither duty binds the Budget Policy Statement or Fiscal Strategy Report. Mechanism lost: a legal requirement to assess and disclose wellbeing (including sustainability for future cohorts) as part of budget strategy, replaced by conventional fiscal-risk and tax-expenditure disclosure.

signals.title: New Zealand RMA Replacement Bills Drop the Statutory Future-Generations Test from Environmental Assessment
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: On 9 December 2025 the New Zealand Government introduced the Natural Environment Bill (234-1) and the companion Planning Bill (235-1) to replace the Resource Management Act 1991. The RMA’s purpose clause (section 5), still in force as at 10 February 2026, defines sustainable management as managing resources in a way that enables people and communities to provide for their well-being while sustaining the potential of natural and physical resources (excluding minerals) to meet the reasonably foreseeable needs of future generations. The Natural Environment Bill’s official explanatory note instead states that clause 4’s purpose is only to establish a framework for the use, protection, and enhancement of the natural environment, and lists goals of enabling resource use within environmental limits, safeguarding life-supporting capacity, protecting human health from contaminants, no net loss of indigenous biodiversity, risk-based natural-hazard planning, and provision for Māori interests — with no future-generations or sustainable-management purpose. The Ministry for the Environment’s RMA-reform page records introduction on 9 December 2025 and an aim to pass the Bills in 2026. As of August 2026 the Bills had been reported back from the Environment Select Committee and given a second reading on 4 August 2026; they had not received Royal assent. Remaining future-generations language in the Planning Bill is confined to identified Māori land being retained for present and future generations of owners, not a general environmental-assessment test.
signals.why_it_matters: New Zealand’s live environmental-assessment statute is one of the few common-law EIA regimes with an explicit future-generations purpose test that consent authorities must apply before granting resource consents. The 2025–26 replacement Bills would repeal that test and substitute limit-setting and development-enabling goals that do not name future generations. Mechanism at stake: RMA s5 currently forces every resource-consent and plan decision to ask whether the rate of resource use sustains resources for reasonably foreseeable future generations; if the Bills pass, that statutory IIA-style criterion disappears from environmental impact assessment. Legal force today is still the RMA; the Bills are a live rollback proposal, not yet law.

signals.summary: On Budget Day 28 May 2026 the Minister of Finance presented the Child Poverty Report 2026 (Te Pōharatanga Tamariki), a statutory companion to Budget 2026. Section 15EA of the Public Finance Act 1989 requires the minister to report to the House on progress against Child Poverty Reduction Act 2018 targets and to indicate whether, and to what extent, Budget measures will affect child poverty. signals.title: Norway’s DFØ Guidance Now Requires Child-Impact Analysis in Pre-Decision Appraisals of State Measures
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: The revised Instructions for Official Studies (utredningsinstruksen), adopted by Royal Decree on 18 October 2024 and in force from 1 November 2024, govern how Norwegian ministries and agencies must appraise state measures before decision. DFØ’s accompanying guide — updated with the revision — now states that when a measure has direct or indirect significance for children, the appraisal 'shall' assess what effects it will have for children so that the best interests of the child are safeguarded. Children are also listed among groups that can raise 'principled questions' under minimum question 3 (alongside Indigenous peoples and minorities). The Children’s Ombudsperson (25 October 2024) treated the new guide as requiring decision-makers to assess consequences for children, hear children and young people, and take a view on the child’s best interests before introducing new measures. The guide is not itself a statute; the Instructions bind the state administration. No 2025–26 law creating a standalone CRIA was found.
signals.why_it_matters: The IIA mechanism is a cross-government pre-decision appraisal duty: ministries must identify who is affected and, where children are affected, assess child impacts and best interests before reforms, regulations or investments are adopted. Legal force is an administrative instruction plus official guidance, not a CRWIA-style statute, but it applies to state measures generally rather than only child-titled bills. signals.title: OECD Youth Policy Toolkit Instructs Governments to Run Youth-Check RIAs and Embed Intergenerational Perspectives in Rulemaking
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: On 26 November 2024 the OECD launched the Youth Policy Toolkit to operationalise the 2022 Council Recommendation on Creating Better Opportunities for Young People. The toolkit's public-governance pillar (Recommendation VI.3) tells governments to embed an intergenerational perspective in rulemaking, budgeting, procurement and infrastructure so present decisions do not compromise future generations. It instructs officials to systematically apply regulatory impact assessments and strategic foresight to age-group and future-generation inequalities, and documents live youth-check models: Austria's Child and Youth Impact Assessment on all new legislative proposals for ages 0-30 (since 2013); Flanders' JoKER child-and-youth report inside RIA for ages 0-25 (since 2008); France's Youth Impact Clause covering youth, intergenerational justice and non-discrimination (since 2009); Germany's Competence Centre Youth-Check, which examined 543 draft bills and published 126 youth-checks between 2017 and 2021; and Parma's January 2024 municipal generational impact evaluation with published guidelines, indicators and participation steps. The toolkit also records the European Commission's 2024 commitment to apply a youth check through Better Regulation tools.
signals.why_it_matters: This is the closest OECD-issued operating manual for Intergenerational Impact Assessment cousins. Mechanism: before a law or regulation is adopted, a named youth-check or RIA step must assess effects on children, young people and (in the French clause) intergenerational justice, using age-disaggregated evidence; legal force ranges from integration inside national RIA systems to a dedicated competence centre. It is not a single binding IIA standard, but it is the first OECD compilation that tells administrations which steps, age bands and institutional owners to copy.

signals.summary: On 24 February 2026 SSB published Notater 2026/7, Generasjonsregnskapet — technical documentation of the generational-accounts model it built for the Ministry of Finance from 2007. The model computes present-value net taxes and transfers by age-sex cohort and a generation equation for long-run fiscal imbalance. The preface states it was used in the National Budget from 2008 through 2013, has not been used in ordinary budget work since, and still rests on that-era data. The 2026 note exists because internal documentation was completed 'in connection with work on a new framework for public finances in the long term' (et nytt rammeverk for offentlige finanser på lang sikt). signals.title: Swedish NIER 2026 Fiscal Sustainability Report Tests Whether Future Generations Face Today's Welfare Bargain
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: On 4 March 2026 Konjunkturinstitutet, a government agency under the Ministry of Finance with a statutory mandate in Act (2007:759), published Fiscal Sustainability Report 2026 (Specialstudie 124). The baseline holds today's tax rules, transfer replacement rates and public-service staffing constant to 2060 and asks whether future generations would still face a welfare system and financing structure broadly similar to today's — the report cites generational accounts (ESO 1995) as the standard approach. NIER judges the baseline sustainable because net financial worth and Maastricht debt do not deteriorate persistently, while stating that a weakening net position 'implies that expenditures are shifted to future generations.' Defence-build-up scenarios to NATO's 3.5% of GDP show that borrowing the increase without budget-strengthening measures keeps net lending negative and the net position on a declining path.
signals.why_it_matters: Sweden's official long-term fiscal test is an OBR-style sustainability IIA with an explicit future-generation incidence rule: NIER must tell the government whether current policy can be continued so later cohorts inherit the same welfare/tax bargain, and it treats rising debt as a transfer onto those cohorts. Mechanism: statutory annual sustainability report to the Ministry of Finance, not a line-by-line Budget IA, but it is the document that scores whether today's fiscal stance fails future generations. Not in the corpus.

signals.title: Wales Makes Long-Term Health Impact Assessments Mandatory for Strategic Public Decisions from April 2027
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: The Health Impact Assessment (Wales) Regulations 2025 (WSI 2025/1215 (W. 198)) were made on 19 November 2025 after Senedd approval and come into force on 6 April 2027. They commence the unused Part 6 power in the Public Health (Wales) Act 2017. Regulation 3 requires listed public bodies to carry out a health impact assessment when proposing a decision of a strategic nature about how to exercise their functions. A HIA is defined as an assessment of likely short- and long-term effects on the physical and mental health of the people of Wales or some of them. Regulation 4 requires the body to identify affected population groups, intended and likely unintended health effects, mitigation or enhancement measures, and to have regard to wider social, economic, cultural and environmental determinants of health and to health inequity factors (including socio-economic status, geography and Equality Act protected characteristics). Regulation 6 requires publication of the HIA as soon as reasonably practicable. Regulation 7 adds further public bodies, including corporate joint committees, Transport for Wales, Social Care Wales and the Welsh Revenue Authority. The Cabinet Secretary's 25 November 2025 written statement says the duty covers 56 organisations, including the Welsh Ministers and local authorities, and is intended to support Well-being of Future Generations (Wales) Act 2015 obligations. Welsh Government supporting information states that a public body that fails to comply may be subject to legal challenge.
signals.why_it_matters: This is a 2025–26 statutory instrument that makes a long-horizon wellbeing-style impact assessment legally mandatory before strategic decisions, rather than another retrospective of the 2015 Well-being Act. Mechanism: specified public bodies, including Welsh Ministers and local authorities, must assess short- and long-term physical and mental health effects, including inequity and wider determinants, before a strategic decision, then publish the assessment. Legal force: Welsh statutory instrument under the 2017 Public Health Act, in force 6 April 2027, with potential judicial review for non-compliance. It is the distinct IIA-cousin regulation the Wales hunt asked for, sitting beside (not replacing) administrative Integrated Impact Assessments used in budget papers.

signals.title: Welsh 2026-27 Budget SIIA Reports Wellbeing Impact Workshops Informed Allocations but Did Not Remove Disproportionate Harms
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: The Welsh Government's January 2026 Strategic Integrated Impact Assessment (SIIA) for the 2026-27 Final Budget is the official tool used to assess spending against equality, sustainability and the Well-being of Future Generations (Wales) Act 2015. For this cycle the SIIA moved from a single draft-budget paper to an interim assessment plus a final assessment, with cross-portfolio workshops after the Draft Budget. The Final Assessment states that those conversations 'directly informed targeted Final Budget allocations', citing among others £5m resource to protect bus services, £5m for apprenticeships, extra FE participation funding, ALN delivery resource, a £112.8m local-government uplift and homelessness-prevention funding, and presents ALN and school-estate case studies as preventative, evidence-led choices. The same document's 'Spending Decisions with Identified Negative or Disproportionate Impacts' section records that the SIIA did not eliminate harms: rail support may be regressive relative to buses; the local-government uplift 'does not fully resolve structural pressures' so councils may still cut social care, ALN and homelessness services affecting children and young people; and extra FE resource is unlikely to clear Level 1/Entry waiting lists, with NEET risk remaining. Corpus rg found no SIIA signal; Audit Wales 'No time to lose' and Senedd Fit for the Future are separate Act-level reviews.
signals.why_it_matters: This is a rare official self-evaluation of whether a future-generations budget IIA actually changes money. Mechanism: ministers must consider cumulative wellbeing, equality and WFG five-ways-of-working impacts before Final Budget adoption, now in a two-stage SIIA. Outcome: the government claims workshop evidence shaped specific allocations (buses, ALN, FE, apprenticeships) while also documenting residual cuts and regressive risks the SIIA did not reverse. It bites at the margin of additional in-year allocations, not as a veto on structurally harmful baselines — consistent with Audit Wales's finding that the Act has not driven system-wide change.

signals.title: World Bank Ships LTGM-HC Toolkit Projecting Cohort Human Capital from 2025 to 2100 for 153 Countries
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: In October 2025 the World Bank posted LTGM-HC v1.0, an Excel human-capital extension of the Long-Term Growth Model; the accompanying Policy Research Working Paper 11276 by Mendes and Pennings is dated December 2025. The toolkit projects workforce human capital from 2025 to 2100 for 153 countries using the Human Capital Index ingredients (learning-adjusted years of pre-tertiary schooling; adult survival; child not-stunted rates) embedded in age cohorts. Users compare reform scenarios (for example raising secondary completion versus test scores) and feed the resulting human-capital growth path into the standard LTGM to see GDP effects. Without new reforms, average human-capital growth slows about 0.15–0.2 percentage points per decade and hits zero around 2080 when today's children retire; a typical reform path almost halves that decline. About two thirds of projected GDP-per-capita gains to 2100 already come from past reforms.
signals.why_it_matters: This is official World Bank human-capital impact-assessment kit, not a legal IIA. Mechanism: before locking education or health reforms, finance and planning ministries can quantify how today's child cohorts change workforce productivity and growth through 2100, making the intergenerational return of underinvestment visible. It does not replace generational accounting of taxes and transfers (no IMF 2025-26 GA manual was found) and is distinct from the May 2026 HCI+ dashboard already in the corpus.

signals.title: Australian Treasury's 2023 Intergenerational Report Is the Current Statutory 40-Year Fiscal IIA; No 2025-26 Federal IGR Yet
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: On 24 August 2023 the Australian Treasury published Intergenerational Report 2023: Australia's future to 2063, the sixth federal IGR, projecting the economy and Budget to 2062-63. The Treasurer's official publication page and the IGR hub still treat 2023 as the current report as of 17 August 2026; no 2025 or 2026 federal IGR has been released. The report is required by the Charter of Budget Honesty Act 1998 Part 6: section 20 obliges the Treasurer to publicly release and table an IGR at least once every five years, and section 21 requires it to assess the long-term sustainability of current Government policies over the following 40 years, including the financial implications of demographic change. The 2023 edition names five structural forces (ageing, digital transformation, climate/net-zero, care demand, geopolitics) and frames budget repair as reducing the debt burden on future generations.

Mechanism: the Treasurer must publish and table a 40-year no-policy-change assessment of whether today's tax-and-spend settings are sustainable for later cohorts, with legal force from Charter of Budget Honesty Act 1998 ss 20-21 (at least every five years). It is not a bill-level gate and does not stop a law, but it is the Commonwealth's only recurring intergenerational budget test. The instrument was on the AU country page and missing from the signal corpus.

signals.summary: Government bill XXVIII/I/69 (Budgetbegleitgesetz 2025), laid in the Nationalrat on 13 May 2025, includes completed Wirkungsorientierte Folgenabschätzung (WFA) Kinder-und-Jugend modules, not simplified 'no material impact' screens. signals.title: German Minijobs Government Draft Drops Jugend-Check Youth-Protective Time-Recording and Payslip Rules
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: KomJC published paired Jugend-Checks on the federal minijobs/minimum-wage package. The 7 February 2022 check of the 1 February Referentenentwurf of the Zweites Gesetz zu Änderungen im Bereich der geringfügigen Beschäftigung identified three youth-relevant effects for 18–27-year-old Minijobbers (1.107 million under-25s in Q3 2021 in the commercial sector): a dynamic Geringfügigkeitsgrenze tied to a 10-hour week at the minimum wage; a new MiLoG § 17 duty for employers to record start, end and duration of daily hours electronically and tamper-proof; and a GewO § 108 duty to print the applicable minimum wage on each payslip. The 3 March 2022 check of the 23 February Regierungsentwurf (then retitled Gesetz zur Erhöhung des Schutzes durch den gesetzlichen Mindestlohn und zu Änderungen im Bereich der geringfügigen Beschäftigung) records that both enforcement clauses had been deleted. KomJC states the dropped electronic record would have made unpaid overtime harder to hide for inexperienced young workers, and the dropped payslip line would have told them the current minimum wage as the earnings cap rose automatically. The dynamic minijob threshold and the 12-euro minimum wage remained. Corpus rg found the KomJC third-report counts signal but no minijobs worked example.
signals.why_it_matters: This is a documented skip of youth-protective clauses after a completed Jugend-Check, not a new toolkit. Mechanism: KomJC, funded by the federal youth ministry, screens every government Referentenentwurf for effects on ages 12–27, sends the check to the lead ministry, and re-checks the cabinet draft; it cannot block a bill. Bite status: skipped. Between 1 and 23 February 2022 the lead labour ministry removed the two IA-identified enforcement rules that KomJC had flagged as specifically useful for young Minijobbers, while keeping the wage-threshold change. The third KomJC report (September 2025) later treats Jugend-Check as non-binding sensitisation and names only BMFSFJ bills that mentioned the check, not BMAS amendments.

signals.title: Hungary Future Generations Deputy Records Act CXI Opinion Duty Was Skipped on T/3613 Spatial Planning Bill
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: The Deputy Commissioner for Future Generations issued a parliamentary figyelmeztetés (attention notice) on bill T/3613, which merged the national, Budapest-agglomeration and Lake Balaton spatial plans into one statute (later 2018. évi CXXXIX. törvény, adopted 12 December 2018). The notice states that Act CXI of 2011 makes protection of future generations the Deputy's task, then records that the proposal did not reach AJBH during administrative consultation, so the Deputy could not judge any attached impact-assessment materials. Public annexes contained no environmental assessment of the plan-type instrument even though Government Decree 2/2005 required one. The Deputy warned MPs that dropping zonal plan-sheets from statute, deleting percentage land-use rules, moving Balaton shoreline rehabilitation plans to ministerial decree, simplifying mining-plot approvals, and letting Government set special rules for priority investments would lower the achieved protection level contrary to Article P and Constitutional Court decision 16/2015 (VI. 5.). No subsequent official page located in this search showing the ministry amended T/3613 in response. Corpus has the Act CXI opinion duty but not this worked skip.
signals.why_it_matters: Hungary's IIA-cousin is the Act CXI section 2(2) duty to give an opinion on draft laws and plans that directly affect future generations' quality of life, before they proceed. Bite status: skipped. On a named spatial-planning bill the promoting ministry did not send the draft to AJBH in administrative consultation, so the statutory opinion gate never ran ex ante; the Deputy could only warn Parliament after tabling. That is primary-source evidence the duty can be bypassed on an irreversible land-use statute, distinct from the later Constitutional Court climate-target annulment already in the corpus.

signals.title: KomJC IKJHG Checks Show Cabinet Dropped a Youth Own-Claim; the Bill Did Not Become Law
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: KomJC published Jugend-Checks on BMFSFJ's Kinder- und Jugendhilfeinklusionsgesetz (IKJHG) at both stages: Referentenentwurf 16 September 2024 (check 24 September 2024) and Regierungsentwurf 27 November 2024 (check 9 December 2024). The instrument is administrative: KomJC screens federal government bills for effects on ages 12–27, sends the check via the youth ministry to the lead unit, and republishes if the cabinet text changes youth impacts. Comparing the two published checks: (1) the Referentenentwurf gave adolescents their own claim to out-of-home Hilfe zur Erziehung; the Regierungsentwurf check's 'Anmerkungen und Hinweise' records that this rule is no longer in the cabinet bill and that keeping it would have strengthened young people's legal standing — cabinet did not follow that youth-positive provision. (2) Help-and-service-plan review: the Referentenentwurf set a 'at latest every two years' interval; the Regierungsentwurf returns to regular review as in current § 36 SGB VIII, which KomJC calls more advantageous for young people because the two-year cap could have stretched reviews. No enacted IKJHG statute was found; KomJC later published a check on a successor 1. KJHSRG Referentenentwurf (stand 23 March 2026, published 22 April 2026). Distinct from the third-report COUNT (490 screens / 91 checks) already in the corpus.
signals.why_it_matters: Mechanism: an independent scientific unit (KomJC) assesses every federal government bill for intended and unintended effects on 12–27-year-olds at Referentenentwurf, may update at cabinet, and publishes the check; the Bundestag is not bound to amend. Bite status: mixed — not followed on the youth own-claim (present in the ministry draft, dropped in the cabinet bill, flagged by KomJC as a loss of youth standing); amended between drafts on the help-plan review interval in a youth-friendlier direction, though KomJC does not prove it caused the change; skipped at enactment (no IKJHG statute; a 2026 successor draft is a different bill).

signals.title: Netherlands Publishes a Completed Generatietoets on the National Circular Economy Programme 2023-2030
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: On 20 March 2025 the Dutch Senate published a completed Generatietoets (dated 18 December 2024, Sira Consulting) on the Nationaal Programma Circulaire Economie 2023-2030, applied to product-lifetime-extension measures for electronics, furniture, textiles, and packaging. The report is the second pilot of the then still-developing instrument: a structured conversation framework scoring expected effects across nine themes, four age bands (<20, 20-45, 45-67, 67+) and two time slices (to 10 years; from 30 years), using a sounding board, expert interviews and non-exhaustive desk research. It finds short-term income losses for working-age groups from higher circular-product prices, employment and health gains, and conditional long-term environment/climate gains that depend on lower consumption volumes. Recommendations to the NPCE include continuing behaviour-change campaigns, using regulation to offset short-term distributional effects, applying the Toets Effecten Ontwikkelingslanden, and digital product passports. The report itself records that the Beleidskompas version of the toets was still forthcoming (expected early 2025). No primary source located that a named NPCE measure was rewritten because of this toets.
signals.why_it_matters: This is the first public completed generatietoets in the GYC corpus — a worked example of the Netherlands' intergenerational IA cousin, distinct from the December 2025 Beleidskompas integration event and from the still-unexecuted Senate motion to attach a generatietoets to the Miljoenennota. Mechanism: a sponsoring-programme assessment of effects on current and future age cohorts before (or alongside) circular-economy policy cycling, using the Leidraad/Beleidskompas toolkit rather than a statutory veto. Legal force is administrative/pilot, not a blocking gate. Bite status: unknown/none-found — the toets issues recommendations but does not document that any NPCE budget line or measure was amended, skipped or repealed.

signals.title: Parma Giunta GC-455-2025 Adopts ANCI VIG Check List 2.0 and Scores the Act Generational
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: On 24 December 2025 Parma's Giunta adopted Delibera GC-455-2025 updating the municipality's Valutazione di Impatto Generazionale (VIG) guidelines. From 1 January 2026 every DUP action plus every delibera and determina must be classified with ANCI Check List 2.0 as generazionale, potenzialmente generazionale, altra misura, or potenzialmente anti generazionale. The act records that a Segretario Generale directive (Prot. 0301903 of 15 November 2024) already made VIG marking mandatory on all delibere and determine from 18 November 2024, and that 31 December 2025 closes the first full year of uniform tagging. PIAO 2025-2027 objective 3.02.08 required the guideline update by that date. The proposing sector scores GC-455-2025 itself as a misura Generazionale under the 17 January 2024 guidelines (GC-16-2024). The four-label scheme is the municipal operating method while national Law 167/2025 DPCMs remain unpublished.
signals.why_it_matters: Mechanism: before a Parma DUP measure, giunta delibera or determina is adopted, the proposing sector must run Check List 2.0 and print a generational label on the act; legal force is administrative (Giunta delibera, immediately executable, plus the 2024 Segretario Generale directive), not the unimplemented national AIR-VIG DPCM. Bite status: this dated official atto actually scores a measure (Generazionale); a second 2025 atto, GC-142-2025 of 11 April 2025 on a local youth council, is also scored Generazionale. No published anti-generational label or skipped/amended measure was found, so decision-change bite remains unknown / not published. Distinct from the May 2025 ANCI national guidelines already in the corpus: this is the first-city operator switching its DUP/delibera tagging to Check List 2.0 after a full year of 2025 marking.

signals.title: Thuringia Publishes a Land Jugend-Check on the Health-Service Bill Now Before the Landtag
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: On 1 July 2026 the Projektstelle Jugend-Check Thüringen (ProJCT) published a full Land-level Jugend-Check on the draft Thüringer Gesetz über den Öffentlichen Gesundheitsdienst (ThürGDG, stand 26 August 2025), the first German Land instrument modelled on the federal KomJC check. ProJCT, at FÖV Speyer and funded by the Thuringian social ministry under cabinet decisions of 23 November 2021 and 6 August 2024 (pilot through end-2026), identifies intended effects on 10–27-year-olds as indirectly affected: § 7(2) naming schools as a setting for ÖGD health-promotion goals, and § 11(3) retaining child-and-youth medical examinations and vaccinations at health offices, especially for young people poorly attached to office-based care. The Thuringian social ministry states the cabinet has adopted the draft and the Landtag is now considering it. ProJCT's homepage also lists other published Land checks, including prisoner-pay reform (draft 27 January 2026; check 27 April 2026) and a 14th Police Tasks Act amendment (13 May 2025). The check describes impacts and does not table numbered 'change §X to Y' recommendations. No Landtag final text comparison was found as of 17 August 2026. Distinct from the federal third-report COUNT already in the corpus, which only mentions the Thuringia pilot in passing.
signals.why_it_matters: Mechanism: during Land government bill drafting, an independent scientific unit (ProJCT) must screen Thuringian cabinet drafts for effects on young people and publish the check so the lead ministry can still amend before Landtag adoption; legal force is a cabinet-pilot administrative duty through end-2026, not a Land statute, and the ministry decides whether to take results up. Bite status: unknown — a completed Land check is public and the bill has moved from draft to cabinet to Landtag, but no enacted text-versus-check comparison is available, and the check itself does not issue binding amendment demands.

signals.title: A.C. 2825 Youth and Civil-Service Bill AIR Omits VIG After Law 167 Entered Into Force
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: On 27 February 2026 the Minister for Sport and Youth presented government bill A.C. 2825 (Disposizioni in materia di giovani e servizio civile universale e deleghe al Governo per il riordino della materia). Senate Bollettino AIR n.18 (January–April 2026, published July 2026) records the AIR as ALLEGATA. The official Camera PDF contains a full Analisi di Impatto della Regolamentazione from page 28, using the DPCM 15 September 2017 n.169 template: synthesis, (1) context, (2) objectives and indicators, (3) options, (4) comparison and impacts including SMEs, (5) implementation and monitoring, (6) consultations, (7) evaluation path. The AIR has no section, annex or heading for Valutazione di Impatto Generazionale (VIG), does not cite Law 167/2025, and does not apply VIG criteria. The bill itself is about youth (ages 14–30), civil service, Carta giovani nazionale and a permanent youth-policy observatory; the AIR discusses ricambio generazionale, NEET, housing and welfare rebalancing as ordinary social impacts. Law 167/2025 Art. 4 excludes only decree-laws from VIG and Art. 4.4 says VIG is in every case necessary where an act has significant social or environmental effects on young people and future generations. A.C. 2825 is an ordinary government bill presented after 29 November 2025, not a decree-law.
signals.why_it_matters: Mechanism: Law 167/2025 requires a preventive VIG inside the AIR on government normative acts other than decree-laws, with methods to be set by a PCM DPCM concerted with the youth authority; Art. 4.4 makes VIG necessary on acts with significant youth/future-generation social or environmental effects. Bite status: this is a completed, named AIR PDF on the government's own youth bill that omits VIG entirely and stays on the 2017 AIR model. That is a skip of the new annex on a dated act, not another recap of the statute. The skip coincides with both implementing DPCMs still being unpublished, so the duty exists on paper while the first post-commencement youth AIR does not run the test. Distinct from italy-vig-generational-impact-assessment-law-2025-11-20 (the November 2025 enactment) and from the Parma/Bologna municipal operators.

signals.title: Flanders Files a Completed JoKER with the Community-Institution School Bill after the 13 March 2026 Age-30 Expansion
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: On 27 May 2026 the Flemish Government laid ontwerp van decreet 864 (2025-2026) No. 1, amending the 17 May 2024 decrees on education in the gemeenschapsinstellingen (closed youth-justice institutions De Zande, De Grubbe and De Kempen). The explanatory memorandum's impact-analysis heading contains a completed JoKER. It treats all young people placed in those institutions as the affected group and, against a nuloptie of the May 2024 three GI-afdelingen model, assesses three chosen measures: one GI-school under a single dedicated director; substantially higher staffing (including ICT and administrative posts so teaching staff can move onto the education statute); and more than doubling the operating budget from EUR 500 per bed. Inwerkingtreding is 1 September 2026 (staff transition 1 August 2026; freedom-restricting measures 7 May 2027). Council of State afdeling Wetgeving advice 78.980/1 of 10 April 2026 (requested 2 March 2026) did not find JoKER missing; listed text changes respond to the Vlaamse Toezichtcommissie, social-partner protocols and CoS remarks on levensbeschouwelijk onderwijs, not to the JoKER. Distinct from corpus id flanders-expands-mandatory-joker-child-and-youth-impact-reports-from-under-25-to-age-30-2026-03-13 (Jeugddecreet 754, filed 19 March 2026).
signals.why_it_matters: Mechanism: before a Flemish Government draft decree that directly affects children and young people is laid in Parliament, Jeugddecreet Art. 7 requires a JoKER in the explanatory memorandum describing effects with the measure, without it, and alternatives to avoid, limit or remedy serious harm; after the 13 March 2026 expansion the statutory cohort is tot en met 30. Bite status: unknown on text — this is a published post-expansion JoKER on a government bill filed 27 May 2026, but the JoKER assesses minors in closed institutions rather than the new 26–30 cohort, CoS did not stall 864 for JoKER, and no article change is attributed to the JoKER.

signals.title: Flemish Council of State Required a Missing JoKER before the 2021 Closed-Supervision Youth-Justice Bill Could Proceed
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: On 18 May 2021 the Belgian Council of State, afdeling Wetgeving, issued advice 69.100/1 on a Flemish voorontwerp amending Article 37 of the 15 February 2019 Jeugddelinquentierecht decree (langdurige gesloten begeleiding for 12–16-year-olds after Constitutional Court arrest 22/2021). CoS recorded that the file contained no kind- en jongereneffectrapport even though the draft unmistakably affected under-25s, held that a 2019 'impactanalyse (inclusief Joker)' on the original decree did not satisfy the new bill, and stated: 'Aan het genoemde vormvereiste zal bijgevolg nog dienen te worden voldaan.' Under the 12 December 2008 BVR a voorontwerp subject to JoKER cannot be approved by the Flemish Government without that report. The government then produced a JoKER dated 20 May 2021 (two days after the advice) and laid the bill on 30 June 2021 as 880 (2020-2021) No. 1, with the JoKER annexed. The annexed JoKER is a completed with/without assessment (nuloptie: no closed supervision for under-16s after the annulment; gekozen optie: restore it for a narrowed list of very serious offences). It does not show the JoKER originating or amending the offence list; that repair was driven by the Constitutional Court. CoS also said Vlaamse Raad WVG advice was still required.
signals.why_it_matters: Mechanism: JoKER is a decree-level form requirement on government draft decrees affecting children and young people; the Youth minister/CJM and the Council of State police it, and the 2008 BVR blocks Flemish Government approval until a JoKER is attached. Bite status: stalled on process, skipped on substance — CoS delayed this dossier at the form-requirement gate until a missing JoKER was written (advice 69.100/1, 18 May 2021; JoKER 20 May 2021; filing 30 June 2021 as 880), but CoS did not refuse to advise and the closed-supervision rules themselves were a Constitutional Court repair, not a JoKER-driven text change.

signals.title: French Agricultural Orientation Law 2025-268 Enacts Youth-Impact-Clause Measures After a Completed 2024 Étude d'Impact
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: The government bill d'orientation pour la souveraineté en matière agricole et le renouvellement des générations en agriculture (NOR AGRS2404686L) was presented to the Council of Ministers on 3 April 2024 with a completed étude d'impact. Every article carries an 'Impacts sur la jeunesse' heading. Filled (not 'sans objet') youth sections include Article 1 (generational farm renewal drawing young and non-farm-origin publics; France Services Agriculture; Pacte 15 December 2023 youth communication), Article 2 (national orientation programme: at least one agriculture-discovery action for every elementary pupil; systematic collège discovery internships; +30% learners in technical agricultural education vs 2022 by 2030), Article 5 (Bachelor Agro bac+3 as a visible youth pathway from BTSA, with insertion and wage-gain figures), and Article 10 (France Services Agriculture as a youth-oriented information and matching network). The COJ 2024 activity report (vie-publique 298489, 14 March 2025) names this bill among six 2024 projets de loi with youth-relevant IAs and records that DJEPVA was seized only on 19 MEAE texts, not this one. After Assemblée first reading (28 May 2024), dissolution, Senate/CMP (18 February 2025) and definitive votes (19–20 February 2025), the bill was promulgated as loi n° 2025-268 of 24 March 2025. Vie-publique's official law page records that the adopted statute keeps the IA youth measures: the national orientation-and-discovery programme (now also covering seconde internships), Bachelor Agro, territorial training-creation contracts, the France Services Agriculture one-stop shop (diagnostics from 1 January 2027), and the 400 000-farm / 500 000-farmer 2035 target. Parliament added a six-month volontariat agricole (Senate) that was not in the IA. Conseil constitutionnel decision 2025-876 DC (20 March 2025) censored 18 articles on other grounds (non-regression of food sovereignty, pesticide/good-faith wording, ZAN cavalier), not the youth-training articles. Corpus has the 2016 circular duty but not this IA-versus-adopted comparison.
signals.why_it_matters: Mechanism: under circulaire 5857-SG of 2 May 2016 and article 8 of loi organique 2009-403, every government bill must carry a clause d'impact jeunesse inside the étude d'impact, analysing equality among young people, intergenerational justice and non-discrimination, including a prospective cohort. The assessor is the drafting ministry; DJEPVA help is optional. Bite status: unknown as to causal amendment — DJEPVA was not seized on this bill, and the youth passages justify the government's own draft rather than an independent check that rewrote an article. Adopted fate is not skipped: the IA-named youth instruments (discovery programme, Bachelor Agro, France Services Agriculture, +30% learner target in the IA/COJ description) were enacted in law 2025-268; Parliament expanded youth-adjacent content (volontariat agricole) instead of dropping the clause's measures.

signals.title: Thuringia Enacts Rechtspfleger Robe Clause After Land Jugend-Check on the Court-Organisation Bill
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: On 29 July 2025 the Projektstelle Jugend-Check Thüringen (ProJCT, FÖV Speyer; cabinet-pilot Land instrument through end-2026) published a full Land Jugend-Check on the draft Gesetz zur Änderung des Thüringer Gerichtsstandortgesetzes und zur Anpassung gerichtsorganisatorischer Regelungen sowie weiterer Zuständigkeitsbestimmungen (stand 8 April 2025). The check identifies intended effects on 18–27-year-old Rechtspfleger as direct addressees: proposed § 4(5) sentence 1 ThürAGGVG would let Rechtspfleger wear Amtstracht in hearings, when pronouncing decisions, and in other procedural acts, which ProJCT says can strengthen young officers' self-confidence and reduce age-based disrespect in conflict situations. About 15–20 Rechtspfleger are appointed in Thuringia each year; 89 Rechtspflegeanwärter were in training in 2024. The Landtag adopted the successor government bill as Drucksache 8/1671. The statute was promulgated as the Thüringer Gesetz zur Anpassung gerichtsorganisatorischer Regelungen und zur Änderung der Zuständigkeit für die Einrichtung der zentralen Überwachungsstelle of 15 December 2025 (GVBl. 2025 Nr. 14 of 22 December 2025, p. 283), in force 30 December 2025. Article 2 enacts § 4(5) in wording that matches the checked clause (hearings and pronouncement sittings; other procedural acts outside the courtroom where appropriate to the standing of the administration of justice; the acting Rechtspfleger decides; the justice ministry regulates design by Verwaltungsvorschrift). Article 1 extends the Bad Lobenstein and Ilmenau amtsgerichtliche Zweigstellen transition from 2025 to 2030. The check describes impacts and does not table numbered 'change §X to Y' recommendations. Distinct from corpus id thuringia-publishes-a-land-jugend-check-on-the-health-service-bill-now-before-the-landtag-2026-07-01, which records the 1 July 2026 ThürGDG check with bite still unknown.

Bite status: not skipped on the youth-relevant clause — the Amtstracht rule ProJCT flagged for young Rechtspfleger was enacted as § 4(5) ThürAGGVG. Causal amendment remains unknown: the check does not issue binding change demands, and the robe clause was already in the 8 April 2025 government draft rather than added after the 29 July 2025 publication.

signals.title: Albania consults on law creating an independent parliamentary Fiscal Council
signals.summary: Albania's Ministry of Finance opened consultation on a draft law establishing the Fiscal Council of the Republic of Albania. The proposed independent body would report to Parliament, assess macro-fiscal forecasts and budget documents, monitor fiscal-rule compliance and public-finance sustainability, and require the Finance Ministry to publicly explain when its recommendations are not followed.
signals.why_it_matters: An independent fiscal institution can expose the future costs of present borrowing, optimistic forecasts and off-budget risks before they become liabilities for younger taxpayers. The proposed comply-or-explain mechanism and parliamentary reporting could strengthen long-term accountability in an EU accession country where fiscal oversight has previously remained within government.

signals.title: Bangladesh launches a 2026–2030 national action plan for safe and regular migration
signals.summary: Bangladesh formally launched its Cabinet-approved National Action Plan 2026–2030 for implementing the Global Compact for Safe, Orderly and Regular Migration. The framework translates GCM commitments into national actions and indicators across evidence-based planning, migrant rights and safety, irregular migration, regular labour mobility and decent work, remittances, and migrant social inclusion. The plan assigns a whole-of-government and whole-of-society implementation approach involving ministries, civil society, employers, migrants and development partners.
signals.why_it_matters: Migration is a central mechanism of generational mobility in Bangladesh, affecting young workers' access to jobs, household remittances and long-term human-capital investment. Turning international commitments into a time-bound national framework could reduce exploitative migration pathways, improve portability and inclusion, and distribute migration's development gains more fairly between migrant workers, their families and future cohorts.

signals.title: Brazil Supreme Court Strikes Compulsory Carbon-Credit Investment Requirement for Insurers
signals.summary: Brazil's Supreme Federal Court unanimously declared unconstitutional Article 56 of Law 15.042/2024, which required insurers, open pension entities, capitalization companies, and local reinsurers to invest at least 0.5 percent of technical reserves and provisions in carbon credits or related funds. In ADI 7795, the court found that the requirement violated free enterprise, equality, legal certainty, and legitimate expectations because it targeted entities without a direct relationship to the largest greenhouse-gas emissions and lacked adequate transition rules.

The resulting country report found that interest payments already absorb about 83% of government tax revenues, gross financing needs are projected near 40% of GDP over the next three years, and stalled divestment and limited maturity extension leave fiscal space for priority social spending constrained despite macroeconomic stabilization.
signals.why_it_matters: The review identifies a concrete long-horizon fiscal burden: exceptionally high interest and refinancing requirements compete with education, social protection, climate resilience and other investments on which younger and future generations depend. Although the IMF does not provide cohort-level incidence, continuing to devote most tax revenue to interest risks transferring reduced public investment, rollover exposure and adjustment costs forward. This Egypt-specific evidence is absent from the current corpus and materially deepens its existing, broader signal on economic anxiety and fiscal policy.

signals.title: Montana Renews Youth Justice Advisory Council With Mandated Young and Tribal Representation
signals.summary: Executive Order 2-2026 continued Montana's Youth Justice Advisory Council within the Department of Justice through March 1, 2028. The 15-to-33-member council reviews the state juvenile-justice plan and grant applications, submits biennial compliance recommendations, and must seek regular input from justice-involved young people. At least one-fifth of members must be under 28, including at least three current or formerly justice-involved members where feasible, while its composition must include a Tribal representative or an expert in Tribal law enforcement and juvenile justice.
signals.why_it_matters: The order preserves a formal, compensated channel through which young and justice-affected people can influence state planning, funding, and oversight rather than participate only through consultation. Requiring both young members and Tribal expertise embeds representation of cohorts facing long-lived consequences from detention, unequal services, and racial disparities into an institution that allocates prevention resources and advises the legislature.

signals.title: Austin Adopts Green Social Housing Evaluation Mandate Built Around Permanent Affordability and Majority City Ownership
signals.summary: Austin City Council adopted Resolution 20260205-047, directing the City Manager to evaluate a comprehensive Green Social Housing policy. The mandated framework combines compact transit-oriented housing, permanent affordability, deeply affordable units below 50% of median family income, tenant participation in development governance, just-cause eviction and rent-escalation protections, carbon and water standards, biodiversity, majority City ownership, and a proposed revolving loan fund that would recycle public capital into additional mixed-income developments. The revolving-finance mechanism could create durable local production capacity, while tenant governance and transit-oriented environmental standards join housing access, democratic participation, mobility, and long-term climate performance in one municipal model. signals.title: Australia Publishes Draft Children’s Online Privacy Code With Deletion, Consent and Geolocation-Notice Rights
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: Australia’s privacy regulator published the exposure draft of the Children’s Online Privacy Code on 31 March 2026. It proposes that covered apps, games, websites, streaming platforms and educational tools treat children’s best interests as a primary consideration, obtain consent for targeted advertising, provide age-appropriate notices, enable children to request destruction of their data, notify children when parents consent on their behalf, and disclose when users—including parents—track their geolocation. The regulator consulted children and young people directly before and after publication, and must register the final legislative instrument by 10 December 2026.
signals.why_it_matters: The draft shifts responsibility from children managing privacy settings to services proving that their data practices serve children’s interests. Its deletion and geolocation-notice provisions recognize young people as rights-holders with privacy and evolving autonomy even where parents participate in monitoring or consent. Because non-compliance with the final code will use the Privacy Act’s regulatory and civil-penalty framework, Australia could supply an accountability model that protects youth participation online without relying only on exclusionary age bans.

signals.title: Australia’s Indigenous Affairs Agency Applies Indigenous Data-Sovereignty Rules to Its AI Governance
signals.summary: The National Indigenous Australians Agency published its 2026 AI Transparency Statement applying Australia’s Framework for Governance of Indigenous Data to agency AI use. NIAA says AI must strengthen Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander community control and protect cultural rights; it currently limits AI to workplace-productivity tools, prohibits AI decision-making, requires authorised human review of outputs, assigns compliance to its CIO, mandates staff training, maintains an AI use-case register and reports high-risk applications. Its planned impact-assessment approach expressly includes cultural-safety risks alongside privacy and security.
signals.why_it_matters: This moves Indigenous data sovereignty from a general public-sector framework into the operating controls of the federal agency responsible for Indigenous affairs. Human review, cultural-safety assessment and community-control requirements can reduce the risk that AI systems appropriate, misrepresent or expose Indigenous knowledge, languages and identity data inherited and maintained across generations. The model is especially relevant to young Indigenous people, whose cultural and digital futures will be shaped by whether government-held knowledge becomes AI training material without Indigenous authority.

signals.title: Slovenia Begins Implementing Pension Reform That Rebalances Adequacy and Ageing Costs Across Generations
signals.summary: Slovenia's ZPIZ-2O pension law began applying on 1 January 2026. It introduces immediate improvements for vulnerable pension recipients and phases in structural changes from 2028 to 2035: retirement thresholds rise from 60 to 62 after 40 contribution years and from 65 to 67 after at least 15 insured years; the pension-base reference period expands from 24 years to 40 years with the five least favourable years excluded; accrual rates increase; and indexation progressively shifts toward inflation.
signals.why_it_matters: The reform explicitly distributes demographic-adjustment costs across cohorts rather than relying only on benefit cuts or higher contributions from younger workers. It combines longer working lives and slower wage-linked indexation with higher accrual rates and stronger protection for lower-income, disability, survivor and future pensioners. The European Commission estimates that the pension measures will reduce long-term pension expenditure by about one percentage point of GDP, while warning that rapid ageing and a shrinking workforce will continue to constrain contribution revenue.

signals.title: South Korea Enacts First National Pension Contribution Support for 18-Year-Olds
signals.summary: On 23 April 2026, South Korea's National Assembly passed a National Pension Act amendment creating a state-funded entry point into the pension system for each new cohort turning 18 from 2027. A young person with no contribution history may apply between ages 18 and 26 for the state to pay the first month's contribution; someone who has already contributed receives an additional credited month. The first eligible cohort is people born in 2009. Establishing a contribution record also allows later make-up payments for gaps caused by study or military service.
signals.why_it_matters: The amendment converts early pension participation from an individual opt-in burden into a publicly supported cohort entitlement. It is a distinct inclusion measure following, rather than duplicating, South Korea's 2025 contribution-rate reform.

signals.title: Tonga Enacts Ocean Management Law Embedding Intergenerational Equity and Climate Resilience
signals.summary: King Tupou VI assented to Tonga's Ocean Management Act 2025 on 16 December 2025. signals.title: UK High Court Upholds National Adaptation Programme but Leaves Path for Individual Climate-Rights Claims
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: In Friends of the Earth and Others v Secretary of State for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, [2024] EWHC 2707 (Admin), the High Court dismissed a challenge to the United Kingdom’s third National Adaptation Programme. It held that section 58 of the Climate Change Act 2008 did not require quantified adaptation objectives or a separate assessment of delivery risk, and that the programme did not breach the claimants’ Convention rights. The court nevertheless indicated that a person directly exposed to extreme heat, flooding or another specific adaptation failure could potentially bring a human-rights claim where the omitted measure fell outside the state’s margin of appreciation.
signals.why_it_matters: The judgment is a significant counter-signal in climate-rights litigation: statutory adaptation duties may permit broad government discretion even where an independent expert body considers the programme inadequate. This clarifies the emerging boundary between general challenges to national adaptation ambition and justiciable rights claims tied to concrete protective measures.

signals.title: New Zealand Passes Parental-Income Test Cutting Jobseeker Support for Most 18- and 19-Year-Olds
signals.summary: A New Zealand Government press release dated Saturday 29 August 2026 states that the Social Security (Jobseeker Support and Accommodation Supplement) Amendment Bill passed its third reading. The Bill implements two Budget 2025 measures: a Parental Assistance Test so that 18- and 19-year-olds (and in specified cases 16- and 17-year-olds) must show parental income below the threshold before receiving Jobseeker Support or the equivalent Emergency Benefit; and a rise in the Accommodation Supplement entry threshold for some homeowners from 30 percent to 40 percent of income. Social Development Minister Louise Upston said the youth rule ‘reinforces the expectation that young people who are not in employment, education or training should be financially supported by their parents, not by taxpayers.’ The government bill text provides commencement on 2 November 2026 for the Jobseeker eligibility part and 1 April 2027 for the housing-subsidy part. October 2025 estimates were that around 4,300 young people would lose eligibility; July 2026 parliamentary answers indicated about 2,733 18- and 19-year-olds on Jobseeker with a health condition, injury or disability, of whom around 70 percent have psychiatric or psychological conditions, would also be in scope unless excluded.
signals.why_it_matters: This is a youth-opportunity rollback using a fiscal-sustainability frame. The mechanism is a parental-means test that shifts income support for unemployed 18- and 19-year-olds from the public budget onto family balance sheets from November 2026. Who benefits now: current taxpayers and older homeowners exempted from the tighter Accommodation Supplement test (superannuitants, veterans and supported-living recipients are carved out). Who pays: young people whose parents earn above the threshold, including many with mental-health conditions who cannot immediately work, and later cohorts if early benefit exclusion raises long-run NEET scarring. The housing change is an intergenerational incidence twist: working-age homeowner subsidies tighten while pensioner homeowners are protected.

signals.title: Romania Environment Ministry Opens Selection for 20-Member Youth Climate and Environment Advisory Council
signals.summary: On 18 August 2026 Romania’s Ministry of Environment, Waters and Forests, the Youth Platform for Sustainability and UNICEF Romania opened selection for the Consiliul Consultativ al Tinerilor privind Clima și Mediul (CCT-CM). The council will have 20 members aged 14–35 from different regions and social backgrounds, tasked with consultations, public-policy recommendations, tracking how those recommendations are treated, and science-based climate communication. Applications close 31 August 2026, members are to be announced 12 September, and the first in-person meeting is scheduled 14–18 September 2026. Environment Minister Diana Buzoianu said today’s climate decisions will shape young people’s future and that their voice needs a standing channel into public policy.

Mechanism: a 20-member advisory council (ages 14–35) with a ministry institutional link, UNICEF child-participation safeguards, and a mandate to formulate recommendations and follow them through decision processes — converting LCOY Romania’s demand for a Youth Advisory Council on Climate Change into an operational participation channel.

signals.title: Scotland Establishes Third Just Transition Commission to 2031 with Adaptation Fairness Mandate
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: On 26 August 2026 the Scottish Government announced the third Just Transition Commission, a 15-member independent body co-chaired by Professor Dave Reay and Satwat Rehman and mandated to run until 2031. The Commission is to advise ministers on how the costs and benefits of climate adaptation and net-zero decarbonisation are shared, produce costed recommendations for the Climate Change Plan and Scottish National Adaptation Plan, and engage workers, rural communities and groups hit hardest by wildfires, flooding and drought. Its remit also covers monitoring and evaluation, early-warning of delivery risks, offshore-energy jobs impacts, and collaboration with international peer bodies. The article was amended on 27 August 2026 to correct a member affiliation and add a link to further Commission information.
signals.why_it_matters: This is a standing fairness institution for who pays now versus later for climate adaptation and industrial decarbonisation. Mechanism: an independent ministerial advisory commission with a 2026–2031 mandate to cost and distribute adaptation and net-zero costs so present workers and future residents do not absorb uncompensated climate and transition burdens. It operationalises just-transition scrutiny after Scotland rejected a statutory Future Generations Commissioner in January 2026, substituting an adaptation-focused commission for a Wales-style wellbeing duty.

signals.title: UN Issue Brief 3 Applies Global Principles for Information Integrity to Children and Youth
signals.summary: On 10 August 2026 the UN Department of Global Communications published Strengthening Information Integrity: Issue Brief 3 — Children, Youth and Information Integrity, the third in a series applying the June 2024 UN Global Principles for Information Integrity, the Pact for the Future and the Global Digital Compact to a specific constituency. The brief records that more than 82 per cent of people aged 15–24 are online, argues that harms to children and youth are produced by attention-and-data business models rather than parental failure, and maps three risk classes (technology-enabled, access/distribution, content-based). Pathways forward require treating children and youth as partners in digital and AI governance, not only as protection subjects, and assign distinct duties to states, technology/AI actors, advertisers, media, researchers and civil society. The accompanying press release cites the Secretary-General’s July 2026 call for an AI Child Safety Pledge: “No child should be a guinea pig for unregulated AI.”
signals.why_it_matters: This is Pact for the Future / Global Digital Compact follow-through at the child-and-youth layer: a UN-system instrument that converts 2024 principles into an operational brief on who bears digital-ecosystem costs now versus who will inherit AI-shaped information environments. The mechanism is multi-stakeholder duty-allocation (states regulate; platforms redesign; youth participate in governance) rather than a new treaty. It fills the corpus gap on information-integrity implementation for minors and supplies a rights-based counterweight to restriction-only social-media bans already tracked.

signals.title: UN Member States Complete Silence Procedure on Sea Level Rise Declaration Affirming Continuity of Statehood
signals.summary: On 20 August 2026 the UNGA President transmitted the final UN Declaration on Sea Level Rise after co-facilitators Australia and Cabo Verde reported that silence procedure was not broken. The four-page text, for adoption at the 24 September 2026 high-level meeting, affirms that maritime zones once established under UNCLOS can be maintained despite physical change, and that disappearance of a constituent element of a State would not necessarily entail loss of statehood, sovereignty, UN membership or associated rights. It cites the ICJ climate advisory opinion and the ILC Study Group report, calls for scaled-up finance for SIDS and LDCs, and decides a further high-level meeting before the end of the eighty-fourth session.
signals.why_it_matters: This is a multilateral legal-political instrument for future generations of climate-vulnerable states, not a scientific communiqué. Mechanism: a consensus General Assembly declaration that locks in continuity of statehood and stable maritime entitlements so later cohorts of island and coastal peoples do not lose sovereignty, resources or UN standing as seas rise. It converts Pacific and AOSIS statehood practice into a UNGA-level presumption, with a scheduled 24 September 2026 adoption and a further review meeting.

signals.title: UNFCCC Issues Fifth Annual Glasgow ACE Implementation Progress Report Ahead of COP31
policy_areas: Monitoring, Audit, Evaluation of policies (+ impact Assessment)
signals.summary: On 27 August 2026 the UNFCCC secretariat issued FCCC/SBI/2026/20 (advance version), the fifth annual summary of progress under the 10-year Glasgow work programme on Action for Climate Empowerment for the period August 2025–July 2026, as a pre-session document for SBI 65 in Antalya (9–14 November 2026). The report records the COP 30 ACE Presidency event, the 2026 ACE Dialogue and technical workshop at SBI 64 that fed the mandated midterm review, secretariat support to the COP 30 and COP 31 PYCCs, Youth4Capacity and Climate Catalysts activities, and regional youth camps and webinars. UNICEF told the Dialogue to strengthen child-responsive ACE, financing and outcome monitoring; workshop participants found ACE more visible in national climate policy but still under-financed, poorly coordinated across ministries, and lacking common impact indicators.
signals.why_it_matters: This is the statutory evaluation layer for the Glasgow ACE programme that the corpus currently holds mainly as a 2021 announcement. ACE (education, training, public awareness, participation, access to information, international cooperation) is the UNFCCC’s main intergenerational-learning instrument; the fifth annual report plus the SBI 64 midterm review are the first systematic check on whether youth and children are being equipped as climate-policy partners or only convened as events. The documented gaps — weak outcome metrics and thin finance — are themselves an implementation finding: process activity is high, measured change for the next generation is not yet evidenced.
